en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men, and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory" (Jaya). Oṃ! Homage to the wielder of the discus, the bestower of all auspiciousness.
For those submerged in the ocean of sense-objects, [he is] the bridge for their deliverance.
Saṃjaya said:
Then those heroes, having gathered together, set out facing the south.
At the hour of sunset, they arrived near the camp;
all of them were then in high spirits.
Having approached the two Pāṇḍavas, Vāsudeva spoke these words.
Having unyoked their mounts, they then became hurried and terrified;
reaching a dense thicket, they entered it and remained hidden,
stationed not very far from the army camp.
Cut down on all sides by sharp weapons and covered in wounds and gashes,
they sighed long and hot,
thinking of the Pāṇḍavas after hearing the terrible roar of the Pāṇḍavas who were seeking victory.
Terrified by the fear of pursuit, they fled once more toward the east.
Having traveled for a short while, those great archers, their mounts exhausted and themselves parched with thirst, could not endure it, falling under the sway of anger and indignation.
Tormented by the slaughter of the king, they stood still for a moment.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, this deed performed by Bhīma is incredible."
"O Saṃjaya, since that son of mine, who possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants,
who was invulnerable to all beings, young, and possessed of a body as firm as a diamond,
has been struck down in battle by the Pāṇḍavas, [my grief is immeasurable]."
"O son of Gavalgaṇa, it is not possible for men to transcend destiny,
since my son, having encountered the sons of Pṛthā in battle, has been struck down.
Surely, O Sañjaya, my heart is made of the essence of stone."
Having heard that his hundred sons were slain, he did not shatter into a thousand pieces;
for how indeed will this aged couple fare, their sons having been killed?
Indeed, I have no desire to dwell in the territory of the son of Pāṇḍu.

"O Sañjaya, how could I, having been the father of the king and being the king myself, now act as a servant by the command of the son of Pāṇḍu? Having once commanded the entire earth and stood upon its very head, O Sañjaya..."
"How shall I exist today as a servant who has brought about my own ruin?
O Sañjaya, how shall I be able to hear the words of Bhīma,
by whom my full hundred sons were slain alone?"
The words of that high-souled Vidura have come true,
O Sañjaya, since my son did not follow his advice.
Now that my son Duryodhana has been slain through unrighteousness, O dear one, [the prophecy is fulfilled].
"10,001.016c What did Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa do, O Sañjaya?
10,001.017 Sañjaya said:
10,001.017a Having gone there, O King, your men halted at no great distance."
They beheld a formidable forest, thick with various trees and creepers.
Having rested for a moment on excellent horses that had found water,
they reached a vast forest at the hour of sunset.
It was frequented by various herds of deer, crowded with various birds,
covered with various trees and creepers, inhabited by various beasts of prey,
filled with various waters, and adorned with ponds.
Covered by hundreds of lotus ponds and filled with blue water-lilies,
they entered that formidable forest and, looking all around,
then beheld a banyan tree shrouded by a thousand branches.
Then, O King, having approached that banyan tree, those great car-warriors,
the best among men, beheld that preeminent lord of the forest. Having descended from their chariots and unyoked their horses, they stood there.
Having sipped water according to the rule, O Lord, they performed their evening devotions.
Then, when the sun had reached the best of mountains, the setting mountain,
night— the sustainer of the entire world— set in.
Adorned by scattered planets, lunar mansions, and stars,
the sky shines like a garment, beautiful to behold on every side;
even those creatures that roam at night stir about only slightly.
Those beings who roam by day fell under the power of sleep;
for those beings who roam by night, there arose a most dreadful clamor. The flesh-eaters were overjoyed, and the terrible night had arrived.
At that terrible onset of night, filled with pain and grief, Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa sat down together. Seated there, they lamented all around the banyan tree.
Having witnessed that very event— the destruction of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas—
they sat upon the surface of the earth with their limbs overcome by sleep,
exhausted by great fatigue, and mangled by various arrows.

Then the two great chariot-warriors, Kṛpa and Bhoja— who were accustomed to comfort and undeserving of suffering— fell under the power of sleep and sat upon the surface of the earth like those who are helpless,
though they were worthy of costly beds.
But those two, O great king, were asleep, overcome by fatigue and grief;
however, O Bhārata, the son of Droṇa, having fallen under the sway of anger and resentment,
did not sleep at all, hissing like a serpent.
Burning with excessive wrath, he could not find sleep;
the mighty-armed one cast his gaze upon that forest of terrible appearance. As he surveyed the region of the forest inhabited by various creatures, he looked about.
The mighty-armed one beheld a banyan tree frequented by crows;
there, O Kauravya, thousands of crows passed that night, sleeping comfortably, each resting in a separate place.
While those crows were sleeping, trusting on all sides,
he suddenly beheld an owl of terrifying appearance approaching—
a creature of great roar and massive body, with tawny eyes and a brownish-piṅgala hue.
With a very long snout and claws, swift as Garuda,
he then made a soft sound like a bird seeking concealment and,
O Bhārata, reached for a branch of a banyan tree.
Having gathered at the branch of the banyan tree,
the bird, the destroyer of crows, slaughtered very many sleeping crows;
he tore off the wings of some and cut off their heads.
The powerful one, whose weapon is his feet, broke the legs of some;
in an instant, he struck down all who stood within the range of his vision. O lord of the people, with their limbs and their bodies, [the ground was covered].
The entire circle of the banyan tree became completely covered on all sides.
Having slain those crows, Kauśika, the slayer of enemies, was filled with joy,
having retaliated against his foes according to his desire.
Having seen that deceitful deed performed by Kauśika in the night,
the son of Droṇa, his resolve formed by that impression, reflected alone:
"Instruction has been given to me by this bird regarding combat."
I consider this the opportune time for me to be intent upon the destruction of the enemies;
however, the Pāṇḍavas cannot be slain by me today,
for they appear victorious, are powerful, full of zeal, have attained their mark, and are skilled strikers.
In the presence of the king, their slaughter was vowed by me. Adopting a course of action like moths entering a fire— which leads to one's own destruction—
there is no doubt that I shall lose my life while fighting according to the rules of righteousness.
Success may indeed be achieved through deception, and there shall be a great destruction of enemies;
for those who are experts in the science of statecraft (arthaśāstra) highly esteem that certain gain which results from a doubtful one.
Whatever may be said here that is censurable and condemned by the world,
that must be performed by a man who lives according to the dharma of the Kṣatriya;
for all things are despised and loathsome at every step.
These very things were prepared with deceit by the Pāṇḍavas, whose self is unrefined.
Regarding this matter, two verses have been sung in the past by those who contemplate dharma, who perceive the truth, and who observe the principles of justice; they are heard [now].
When the enemy force is exhausted, shattered, or even while they are eating;
during their departure or their entry—then one should strike the enemy's army. Likewise, when they are afflicted by sleep at midnight, or when they have lost their leader.
An army whose warriors are divided and which is split in two should not be regarded by the wise as fit for the destruction of the enemy;
rather, one should employ whatever means necessary to slay the foe.
One who observes justice should never kill an enemy; yet,
if it were possible to cut an enemy down from the very root,
one should exert effort toward that end so that such success may be achieved.
Thus did the powerful son of Droṇa resolve upon the slaughter of the sleeping Pāṇḍavas along with the Pañcālas; meanwhile,
those two high-souled and mighty heroes, Kṛpa and the Bhoja, awoke.
Having adopted a cruel resolve and deliberated upon it again and again,
he awakened those two who were asleep— his maternal uncle and the Bhoja. Overcome with shame, however, he could find no fitting reply in that situation.
Having meditated for a moment, he spoke, overwhelmed with tears:
"King Duryodhana has been slain— the sole hero of great strength,
for whose sake this enmity was undertaken by us against the Pāṇḍavas."
Alone in battle against many base warriors, that leader of eleven armies of pure prowess was struck down by Bhīmasena. This most cruel deed has been committed by the base Vṛkodara.
As he trampled with his foot upon the head of the consecrated king,
the Pāñcālas roared, shouted, and laughed; filled with joy,
they blew conchs by the hundreds and struck their drums.
The tumultuous sound of musical instruments, mingled with the blare of conchs,
driven by the wind, was indeed terrible as it seemed to fill the quarters of the sky;
so too the neighing of horses and the trumpeting of elephants.
This very great lion-roar of the heroes is heard,
as they, filled with joy, are shouting loudly while stationed toward the eastern direction;
and the hair-raising sounds of chariot wheels are also being heard.
Since this slaughter of the Dhārtarāṣṭras was carried out by the Pāṇḍavas,
we alone remain as the three survivors of that great carnage.
Some of us possessed the strength of a hundred elephants, while others were experts in all weapons.
"Slain by the sons of Pāṇḍu, I consider this to be the reversal of Time. Indeed,
this must surely have been the true course of events,
since such was his end even after accomplishing a difficult task."
"If your wisdom has not been impaired by delusion, then tell us what is for our highest good now that this great purpose of ours has gone astray. Kṛpa said:
"O Lord, O mighty-armed one, you have heard all my words, which are consistent with reason. Now, however, hear a few words from me as well:
all human beings are bound by the constraints of two types of karma."
In destiny and human effort, there is nothing superior to these two.
For actions are not accomplished by destiny alone, O best of beings, nor even by action alone; success comes from the union of both.
By both of these, indeed, all objects—whether inferior or superior—are bound;
they are seen to proceed in every way and likewise to cease in every way. Nor is there any accomplishment whatsoever through human effort alone.
What fruit does Parjanya produce by raining upon a mountain? Likewise, what fruit does he produce by not raining upon a ploughed field?
For there is success through human effort even without divine favor, and divine favor even for one who lacks human effort.

In every case, it becomes useless; what certainty can there be in that? Just as when the rain has fallen and the field has been properly ploughed, the seed may possess great qualities, so too does human success arise.
Having determined the role of destiny between those two, it proceeds according to its own power;
however, the wise, relying on skillfulness, apply themselves to human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
For by means of these two, O bull among men, all the purposes of human actions are accomplished.
They are seen exerting themselves, and likewise they are seen desisting;
even when human effort has been made, it succeeds only through destiny.
Thus, the fruit of this action comes to fruition for the doer.

The exertion of industrious men, even when perfectly executed, is seen in this world to be fruitless if it is devoid of destiny. In that regard, those among men who are indolent and lacking in resolve [fail].
The wise censure such exertion; it does not please them,
for generally, an action performed is seen to be fruitless on this earth,
whereas an action left undone may be seen to yield great fruit.
If one who makes no effort obtains anything by chance,
or if one who has made effort obtains nothing, both of them are in a miserable state.
A skillful person is able to live, whereas a lazy person does not prosper in happiness.
In this world of living beings, those who are capable are generally seen to be seekers of welfare.
If a capable person does not obtain the fruit of his undertakings through his actions, he should not be blamed for anything; rather, he attains the essential truth.

He who, standing idle in this world, obtains fruit without having performed the work, incurs censure and generally becomes an object of hatred. He who disregards this and conducts himself otherwise [is likewise].

He brings about his own misfortune; this is not the way of the wise. When [an effort] is deficient in either human exertion or destiny, then through these two causes, one's enterprise will be fruitless.
An action that lacks human effort does not succeed here; however, he who pays homage to the deities and pursues his goals correctly—
with skill and endowed with courtesy— is never frustrated in vain.

10,002.021a Furthermore, right effort consists in this: that one serves the elders, 10,002.021c inquires after what is beneficial, and acts upon their wholesome advice. 10,002.022a For rising again and again, one should always consult those esteemed by the elders.

That is the supreme root of his yoga; success is said to have that as its root. For he who, having heard the words of the elders, applies himself to exertion, will soon obtain the full fruit of that exertion.
If a man seeks wealth out of passion, anger, fear, or greed,
being powerless and contemptuous, he is swiftly deprived of his fortune.
This very wealth has been sought by the greedy and short-sighted Duryodhana.
Having undertaken an impossible task out of folly without due reflection,
and disregarding those with well-meaning intentions after consulting with the wicked,
he provoked enmity with the Pāṇḍavas, who were far superior in virtue, even though he was being restrained.
Even though he was previously of exceedingly wicked character, he ought not to be treated with such wretchedness;
for when one's purpose has failed, it burns the heart that the advice of friends was not followed.
As for the fact that we have followed after that sinful man—
Because of this, this great and terrible misfortune has now befallen even us. Yet,
my mind, though tormented by this calamity and reflecting upon it, does not perceive what is for my own ultimate good.
But when a man is bewildered, he should consult wise friends;
therein his intellect and discipline find their focus, and therein he perceives what is beneficial.
Then, having determined the root of his affairs through his intellect, those wise ones [should act].
Whatever they may say when questioned, that must be done accordingly. Therefore, having approached Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, and the high-minded Vidura, we shall consult them.
"If they are questioned, they should say: 'Whatever is for our immediate welfare must be performed by us again'; this is my firm conviction.
For without undertaking actions, no purpose is ever accomplished."
"But for those whose undertaking does not succeed even when human effort has been exerted, they are struck down by fate; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. Sañjaya said:
Having heard these auspicious words of Kṛpa, which were consistent with righteousness and worldly purpose,
O great king, Aśvatthāman was filled with pain and grief,
burning as if with a blazing fire.
Then, having made his mind cruel, he addressed them both:
"In every individual, there arises a particular understanding that seems beautiful;
and all people are satisfied with their own respective wisdom."
For everyone in the world considers themselves more intelligent;
to everyone, their own self is highly esteemed, and everyone praises their own self.
For indeed, everyone’s own wisdom is firmly established in its own praise.
They disparage the wisdom of others and repeatedly praise themselves; yet,
when their minds are in agreement regarding the application of different means for yoga,
they take pleasure in one another and hold each other in high esteem again and again.
But for that very same person, those various thoughts,
encountering the reversal brought about by the conjunction of time, perish one after another;
for the thoughts of men are indeed inconceivable, especially so.
Having encountered a deficiency of mind, that particular cognition arises.
For just as a skilled physician, O Lord, having diagnosed a disease according to the rules,
prepares a remedy through proper application for the sake of its pacification in this world.
In this way, men apply their intellect for the sake of accomplishing their tasks;
yet, though endowed with their own wisdom, men disparage that very intellect.
For in youth, a mortal is deluded by another kind of understanding.
In the midst of one kind of old age, he finds pleasure in another; moreover,
O Bhoja, having encountered either a terrible calamity or a similar prosperity, a man undergoes a transformation of his intellect.
In one and the same person, various such cognitions arise from time to time;
because his wisdom is impermanent, he does not find satisfaction in any one of them.
However, having reached a certainty according to his wisdom, he regards that particular view as excellent.
She directs her affection toward him, and she is the one who impels his exertion.
For every man, O Bhoja, having become certain that "this is good," begins to act with pleasure even in deeds such as those leading to death.
For all men, having understood reason and their own wisdom,
engage in various activities, knowing them to be for their own benefit;
yet this mind of mine, born today from calamity, has arisen.
I shall declare to you both that [discourse] which destroys my grief.
Having created living beings and assigned duties to them, Prajāpati established one most excellent quality for each of the social orders (varṇas).
In a Brāhmaṇa, undistracted self-control; in a Kṣatriya, supreme splendor;
in a Vaiśya, skillfulness; and in a Śūdra, conformity to all the castes. A Brāhmaṇa who lacks self-control is wicked, and a Kṣatriya devoid of splendor is base.
A Vaiśya who lacks skill is indeed censured, as is a Śūdra who acts contrary [to his duty].
Yet I have been born into a most excellent and highly honored family of Brāhmaṇas;
through my misfortune, however, I have followed this dharma of the Kṣatriyas.
"If, having understood the duty of a Kṣatriya, I were to perform a very great deed while not relying on my status as a Brāhmaṇa, that would not be considered right by me—
especially after wielding a divine bow and divine weapons in battle."

"Having seen my father slain, what indeed shall I say in the assembly? Therefore, today, having followed that duty of a Kṣatriya according to my desire, I shall go the way of the king, my father of great luster."
Today the Pāñcālas will sleep confidently, appearing as victors; having unyoked their draft animals and removed their armor, they are filled with joy.
Today, all of them, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, shall be slaughtered.

"We have been defeated and considered conquered by them; we are exhausted from this exertion. While they are sleeping soundly at night in their own camp, I shall today launch a difficult assault upon that camp."
Having leaped upon those senseless ones who have become like ghosts in their camp,
I shall slay them with valor, just as Maghavan [Indra] slew the Dānavas; today, I shall strike all of them together, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Exerting my prowess, I shall consume them like a blazing fire consuming dry grass;
O best of men, having slain the Pāñcālas, I shall find peace.
Today, I shall roam among the Pāñcālas in battle, slaughtering them.
Like Rudra himself, enraged among his sacrificial victims, the wielder of the Pināka bow will act today. Having struck down and torn apart all the Pāñcālas,
I shall then follow today the difficult path of the five [Pāṇḍavas].
Enraged, I shall likewise afflict the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle;
and with great joy, I shall slaughter them like animals, as the wielder of the Pināka bow does.
Today, I shall turn the entire earth into a landscape of embodied beings by means of all the Pañcālas.
By striking them down one by one, I shall discharge my debt to my father,
as well as to Duryodhana, Karṇa, Bhīṣma,
and the ruler of the Sindhus; today I shall send the Pāñcālas upon the difficult path that awaits them.

Today, at night, during the final watch, I shall forcibly crush the head of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the king of the Pañcālas, like that of a sacrificial animal. Today, I shall [crush] the sons of the Pañcālas and the Pāṇḍavas as they sleep at night.
"O Gautama, I shall crush you in battle with my sharpened sword at the end of the night;
O Gautama, I shall crush you with my sword in the darkness of the night.
Today, having struck down that army of the Pañcālas while they sleep in the night."
"O high-minded one, I shall have fulfilled my purpose and become truly happy.
It is heard that in the past, the son of Jamadagni, unable to endure the slaughter of his father,
cleared the earth of the Kṣatriya caste twenty-one times."
Kṛpa said:
"By good fortune, O Acyuta, this resolve has arisen in you regarding how to retaliate;
even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself would not be able to restrain you."
"Tomorrow at dawn, we two shall follow you together;
for tonight, rest, having laid aside your armor and banner.
I myself and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata shall follow behind you."
"O best of chariot-warriors,
tomorrow in the encounter, clad in armor and mounting our two chariots, you shall advance against the enemy and, exerting your prowess, slay the Pāñcālas along with their followers together with us."
"You are capable of exerting your prowess; rest for this night.
You have been awake for a long time, my dear; therefore, sleep for this night. Once rested, free from drowsiness, and with a composed mind, O giver of honor,"
Having encountered your enemies in battle, you will slay them; of this there is no doubt.
For among the gods, not even the son of Agni would dare to conquer you, O best of chariot-warriors, when you have grasped your excellent weapons.
Who, even the King of the Gods himself, could fight in battle against the son of Droṇa when he is enraged, accompanied by Kṛpa and joined by Kṛtavarman? Thus,
we have become fully rested, free from sleeplessness, and rid of our feverish distress.
"When night has turned to dawn, we shall surely slay our enemies;
for there is no doubt that you possess divine weapons, as do I,
and likewise the Sātvata, that great archer who is ever skilled in battles."
"O dear one, having forcibly slain all those assembled enemies together in battle, we shall attain abundant joy. Therefore, rest undisturbed and sleep happily this night."
"O best of men, Kṛtavarman and I, both archers who scorch our enemies, shall follow you together as you advance,
having mounted our chariots and clad in armor, following you, the chariot-warrior, as you proceed with haste."
Having gone to their camp and proclaimed your name in battle,
you shall then cause a great slaughter of the enemies as they fight. And having wrought that slaughter among them on the clear morning of the day, [you shall act].
Dwell here as Śakra did after slaying the great Asuras;
for you are indeed capable of conquering the army of the Pañcālas in battle,
just as the enraged destroyer of all Dānavas conquered the host of the Daityas.
Even the Lord himself, the wielder of the thunderbolt, could not withstand you when you were joined by me and protected by Kṛtavarman in battle. Nor,
O dear one, could I, nor likewise Kṛtavarman, [withstand you] in combat.
"Without having conquered the Pāṇḍavas in battle, we shall never retreat;
and having slain those base Pañcālas along with the Pāṇḍavas in combat,
we shall all either return or go to heaven as slain."
"By every possible means, we ourselves shall be your allies at dawn;
O mighty-armed, sinless one, I tell you this truth.
Having been thus addressed by his maternal uncle with these beneficial words, the son of Droṇa [then acted].

10,004.020c Rolling his eyes in anger, O King, he said to his maternal uncle: 10,004.021a "How can there be sleep for a man who is afflicted, or for one who is indignant, or for one who is brooding over wealth, or again, for one who is full of desire?"
Behold, these four things have now come upon me today;
even a fourth part of them would destroy my dream in an instant. What indeed could be more painful in this world than to remember the slaughter of my father?
Burning my heart today, it does not subside by day or night.
Just as my father was especially struck down by the wicked—
though you witnessed all of it with your own eyes— that memory cuts through my very vitals.
"How indeed can one such as I live in this world for even a moment,
when I hear the words of the Pāñcālas that Droṇa has been slain? Without slaying Dṛṣṭadyumna in battle, I have no desire to live."
Because of the slaughter of my father, he— and those Pāñcālas who have gathered together— are to be slain by me.
Furthermore, that lamentation of the king with his thighs broken which I heard—
whom, even among the cruel, would it not burn to the heart?

For whose eyes, even if devoid of compassion, would not flow with tears upon hearing such words again from the king whose thighs were broken? And as for this circle of my friends who has been defeated while I yet live—
This increases my grief, like a torrent of water swelling the ocean.
With my mind so intensely focused today, whence can there be sleep, and whence can there be happiness?
For those [sons] were protected by both Vāsudeva and Arjuna.
"O uncle, I consider them most difficult to withstand even by Mahendra himself;
nor am I capable of being restrained from this task by any means whatsoever.
I do not see anyone in this world who could turn me back from my purpose."
10,004.031e Thus is my mind resolved, and this is approved as virtuous by me;
10,004.032a however, the defeat of my friends being recounted by the messengers,
and the victory of the Pāṇḍavas, burns my heart as it were.
"Having caused the slaughter of my enemies tonight while they sleep, I shall then rest and sleep, free from all anxiety. Kṛpa said:

Even a man who is intent on listening, if he is dull-witted and has his senses unrestrained, is not capable of fully understanding both dharma and artha; this is my opinion. Likewise, even a wise person who does not train himself in discipline [is likewise incapable].
And he does not understand even the slightest determination of the meaning of the Dharma;
for even after attending upon a wise man for a long time, that dull-witted hero does not comprehend the teachings, just as a ladle cannot taste the flavors of the soup.

Even by attending upon that wise man for but a moment, the learned person quickly understands the principles of dharma, just as the tongue perceives the flavors of well-prepared soups. Indeed, it is the intelligent man who is intent on service and has his senses restrained [who attains this].
One should understand all the scriptures and not contradict what is to be accepted.
But that evil-souled, wicked man who is unleadable and contemptuous,
having cast aside what is ordained as auspicious, performs much that is sinful.
Friends restrain one who has a protector from committing a sin;
indeed, the fortunate man turns back, but the unfortunate man does not turn back.
For just as a person whose mind is distracted is restrained by various kinds of words, so too is he turned back.

In the same way, one who is capable can help a friend, but one who is incapable only brings about his own exhaustion. Likewise, when a wise man is performing a wicked deed, wise friends restrain him again and again to the best of their ability.

Having set your mind on what is wholesome and having restrained yourself by your own self, O dear one, follow my word so that you do not suffer later. In this world, according to the dharma, the killing of those who are asleep is not honored.
Likewise, those who have laid down their weapons, those who have abandoned their chariots and horses,
those who say "I am yours," those who have come for refuge,
those with disheveled hair, and those whose mounts have been slain.
"O Lord, today the Pāñcālas will sleep with their armor laid aside;
all of them, trusting in the night, will sleep like senseless spirits.
Any crooked man who would do harm to them in that state—"
It is evident that he would sink into a bottomless and vast hell without a raft;
for you are renowned as the best in the world among those skilled in all weapons,
and not even the slightest fault has ever been found in you in this world.
But you, resplendent like the sun, when the sun has risen tomorrow,
shall be the illuminator of all beings and the conqueror of your enemies in battle;
for a contemptible deed is inconceivable in you.
"It would be like red dye applied to a white cloth; such is my thought.
Aśvatthāman said:
"It is exactly as you have said, O maternal uncle; I shall instruct you here accordingly."
By them, however, this bridge was previously shattered into a hundred pieces,
even in the presence of you kings and within your sight;
my father, having laid down his weapons, was struck down by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
And Karṇa, the best of chariot-warriors, when the wheel of his chariot had sunk and he was overcome by supreme calamity,
was slain by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Likewise, Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, having laid down his weapons and being unarmed, [was slain].

Placing Śikhaṇḍin at the forefront, the great archer Bhūriśravas was slain by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow; likewise, while he was lying on the field of battle in the *prāya* posture, he was struck down by Yuyudhāna amidst the cries of the kings.
And Duryodhana, having encountered Bhīma with a mace in battle,
was struck down unrighteously while the protectors of the earth looked on;
there, being alone, he was surrounded by many great chariot-warriors.
By Bhīmasena, that tiger among men, he was struck down through unrighteous means.
The lamentation of my king, whose thighs were broken, which I have heard from the messengers as they recounted it,
cuts into my very vitals.
"Thus these unrighteous and sinful Pāñcālas have broken the bridge of dharma;
why do you not censure them who have thus transgressed the bounds of propriety?
I shall instead go to offer my respects to the Kuru king, my father."
Having slain the Pāñcālas, the murderers of my father, in a nocturnal ambush,
I would rather become a worm or a moth at will upon taking birth;
I am in haste today to accomplish this which I desire to do.
For me, who am thus hurrying, whence can there be sleep, and whence can there be happiness? No man has ever been born in this world, nor will there ever be one,
who could turn back this resolve of mine regarding their slaughter.
10,005.028 Sañjaya said:
10,005.028a Having spoken thus, O Great King, the powerful son of Droṇa,
10,005.028c having harnessed his horses in a secluded spot, set out toward the enemy.
Both the high-souled Bhoja and Śāradvata said to him: "O bull among men, why is this chariot yoked? What is it that you intend to do?
For we two have set out on this same journey together with you."
"You should not suspect us, for we are indeed equal in both sorrow and joy.
But Aśvatthāman, enraged and remembering the slaughter of his father,
then told them the truth regarding what he intended to do for himself.
Having slain hundreds of thousands of warriors with sharpened arrows,
my father— having laid down his weapons— was struck down by Dhṛṣṭadyumna. In that very same manner, I shall surely slay him today once he has laid aside his armor.

"How was the wicked son of the Pāñcāla king slain by me through a sinful deed? It is my conviction that this wicked Pāñcāla should attain those worlds that are forbidden to one who has abandoned weapons in battle."
"Quickly, having donned your armor and girded yourselves with swords, take up your excellent bows and mount your chariots; wait there, you two subduers of enemies.
Having spoken thus, he mounted his chariot and set out toward the enemy.
O King, Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata followed him. As they advanced toward the enemy, those three shone like kindled sacrificial fires being offered oblations at a sacrifice.
And they went to their camp, O Lord, where the people were fast asleep;
but having reached the gateway, the son of Droṇa stood upon his excellent chariot.
Sañjaya said:
Then Vāsudeva and the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), having reached an agreement and being resolved upon the slaughter of those Pāñcālas, both great observers of vows,
[Arjuna] spoke to Mahādeva, Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds.

"Having assumed the form of Yoga, I shall enter the inner mind; then, being thus prepared, I will accomplish this task directly. Having formed this resolution, they remained there, each possessing a single form.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, tell me what Bhoja and Kṛpa did after they saw the son of Droṇa stationed at the gateway."
10,006.002 Saṃjaya said:
Having addressed Kṛtavarman and the great car-warrior Kṛpa,
the son of Droṇa, his soul overwhelmed with wrath, approached the gate of the camp.
There he saw a being of massive body, with a radiance like that of the moon and sun, standing blocking the gate and causing one's hair to stand on end;
it was wearing a tiger skin dripping with great quantities of blood.
He had a black antelope skin as his upper garment and a serpent as his sacred thread;
with his long, thick arms raised, brandishing various weapons,
he wore great serpents as armlets, and his face was wreathed in garlands of flames.
With a face made terrible by fangs and a gaping mouth that inspires fear,
adorned with thousands of diverse eyes,
his physical form or even his attire cannot be described.
In every way, even the mountains would shatter upon beholding him;
from his mouth, from his two nostrils, from his two ears,
and from all those thousands of eyes, great flames burst forth on every side.

Likewise, from the rays of light, hundreds and thousands of Hṛṣīkeśas appeared, bearing conchs, discs, and maces. Beholding that most wonderful occurrence, which struck terror into the worlds, [the gods were amazed].
The son of Droṇa, remaining unperturbed, covered him with showers of celestial weapons;
but that great being devoured those arrows released by the son of Droṇa,
just as the submarine fire at the mouth of the Vaḍavā swallows the surging waters of the ocean.
In that manner, he swallowed up those arrows discharged by the son of Droṇa.
But Aśvatthāman, beholding those volleys of arrows rendered useless,
released at him a chariot-spear that blazed like a flame of fire.
Then that chariot-spear, with its blazing tip, shattered upon striking him,
like a great meteor fallen from the sky after striking the sun at the end of an eon.
Then [he seized] a divine sword with a golden hilt, possessing the luster of the sky.
He quickly drew [the sword] from its scabbard like a blazing serpent from its hole;
then the wise one hurled that excellent sword at the *bhūta*. Upon reaching that *bhūta*, it indeed dissolved like a tuft of cotton.
Then the enraged son of Droṇa hurled at him a blazing mace resembling the banner of Indra, but that being swallowed it as well. Then, seeing that all his weapons were gone, he looked here and there.
He saw that the sky, which had been clear, was now filled with Janārdanas;
seeing that most wonderful sight, the son of Droṇa, deprived of his weapons and deeply distressed,
spoke while recollecting the words of Kṛpa.

He who does not listen to his friends when they speak what is unpleasant yet beneficial will grieve when he encounters calamity, just as I have done after overstepping those two. He who, disregarding the rules of the scriptures, seeks to kill those who should not be slain, will surely suffer.

10,006.020c He falls away from the righteous path and enters upon a wrong path. 10,006.021a [He commits offenses] against cows, Brahmins, kings, and women; likewise against a friend, a mother, and a teacher;
and against the elderly, children, the mentally dull, and the blind, as well as those who are asleep, terrified, or just arisen.
"One should not brandish weapons against those who are intoxicated, insane, or heedless"—
this has always been taught by the elders to men. Yet I have transgressed that eternal path shown by the scriptures.
Having thus begun by an improper path, one falls into a terrible calamity;
and the wise declare that calamity to be even more dreadful when,
having undertaken a great task, one turns back out of fear.
Who here is able to accomplish that which is impossible, even by the power of one's own strength? Indeed, human effort is said to be more important than destiny;
for if, while performing human action, it does not succeed due to destiny, [it is still better than inaction].
He who has strayed from the path of dharma encounters calamity;
for the wise declare that an unknown obstacle arises when one,
having begun some action, desists out of fear in this world.
"Because of this ill-advised act, this fear has come upon me;
for the son of Droṇa would never retreat from battle under any circumstances.
And this great being has appeared, like the raised rod of fate."
Even though I reflect upon it in every way, I do not recognize this;
surely this foul-mindedness of mine that has turned toward unrighteousness is destined for this terrible fruit, which now appears as my own destruction.
"This turning back of mine in battle has been ordained by fate;
it is not possible to exert oneself here in any way other than through fate.
Therefore, today I seek refuge with the Lord Mahādeva."
"For he will surely destroy this terrible divine punishment of mine. Therefore, take refuge in Kapardin, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā—
Rudra, the wearer of a garland of skulls, Hara, who destroyed the eyes of Bhaga."
"For that god has surpassed all other gods by means of his ascetic power and his prowess;
therefore, I shall seek refuge with Giriśa, the wielder of the trident.
Saṃjaya said:
Having reflected thus, O lord of the people, the son of Droṇa descended from the seat of his chariot and stood there with restrained mind, lost in thought.
The son of Droṇa said:
The fierce Sthāṇu, Śiva, Rudra, Śarva, Īśāna, Īśvara, Giriśa, the boon-granting god Bhava, the creator Bhāvana, the imperishable one,
the blue-throated one, the unborn, Śakra, Kratha, the destroyer of sacrifices, and Hara.
To Viśvarūpa, Virūpākṣa, Bahurūpa, the Lord of Umā;
to the one who dwells in the cremation ground, the haughty, the Great Gaṇapati, the Sovereign;
to the bearer of the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), the shaven-headed, the one with matted locks, the celibate student (brahmacārin).
Even with a mind that is impure in thought, difficult to control, and small in scope,
I shall worship the Destroyer of Tripura by offering myself as a sacrifice—
him who is praised, worthy of praise, and being praised, the one whose actions are never in vain, the one clothed in skin.
Vilohita, Nīlakaṇṭha, the Uncompounded, the Irresistible,
Śukra, the Creator of the Universe, Brahman, and indeed the Brahmachārī;
the observer of vows, eternally devoted to austerity, the Infinite, and the goal of those who practice asceticism.
He who possesses many forms, the leader of the hosts, the three-eyed one, beloved by his attendants; whose face is gazed upon by the leader of the hosts, the darling of Gaurī’s heart;
the father of Kumāra, the tawny-hued one, whose vehicle is the preeminent bull.
He was lightly clad, exceedingly fierce, and devoted to the adornment of Umā;
he was the supreme among the supreme, the highest beyond whom nothing exists,
the wielder of the best of arrows and weapons, and the very limit of the southern quarter.
I take refuge with the highest concentration in the god who wears golden armor and is adorned with the moon upon his crest; through this,
may I cross over this terrible and most difficult-to-traverse calamity today.
"I shall sacrifice to the Pure One with pure offerings of all living beings.
Knowing this resolve of his, that mind characterized by renunciation,
a golden altar appeared before that high-souled one.
O King, at that time, the fire was born upon that altar,
filling the heavens, the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the sky with its flames;
it appeared as if bearing armlets variegated with jewels and raising its hands on high.
There appeared beings with blazing mouths and eyes, possessing many feet, heads, and arms;
resembling elephants and mountains, they had massive faces.
Some had the forms of dogs, boars, and camels, while others had the faces of horses, jackals, and cows.
Some had the faces of bears and cats, while others had the faces of tigers and leopards;
some had the faces of crows, others the faces of monkeys, and likewise the faces of parrots;
some had the faces of great pythons, and others the faces of swans, radiant with white light.
O Bhārata, there were those with faces like woodpeckers and those with faces like blue jays;
hundreds and thousands of them had eyes like Indra’s, as well as pot-bellied ones,
and others with faces like tortoises, crocodiles, and porpoises.
Some had the faces of great sea-monsters (makara), and likewise those of whales (timi);
some had the faces of lions, the faces of curlews (krauñca), and similarly the faces of pigeons and elephants;
some had the faces of doves (pārāvata) and likewise the faces of water-fowl (madgu).
O Bhārata, there were those with hands for ears, those with a thousand eyes, and likewise those with a hundred bellies; they were fleshless, with faces like crows and faces like hawks;
and similarly, O King, there were headless beings and terrifying ones with the faces of bears.
O Indra among kings, some had blazing eyes and tongues, and likewise faces of flame; others had hair of fire, O lord of men, with four arms and hair that was aflame;
and still others, O King, had the faces of rams or the faces of goats.
They had the luster of conchs, faces like conchs, and likewise ears like conchs;
they were adorned with garlands of conchs and possessed voices identical to the sound of a conch.
Some wore matted hair, some had five tufts of hair, while others were shaven-headed or had lean bellies.
O king of kings, they had four fangs and four tongues, spike-like ears, and wore diadems; some bore crowns and others had curly hair;
they were turbaned and crowned, with beautiful faces and well-adorned.

Some wore beautiful earrings and likewise bore crowns; some carried garlands of lotuses and water-lilies, while others bore lilies. Endowed with great majesty, they appeared by the hundreds and thousands.

O Bhārata, they held *śataghnīs* and discs in their hands, as well as maces; some carried *bhuśuṇḍīs* and nooses, and others carried clubs. With quivers fastened to their backs and carrying variegated arrows, they were fierce in battle.
They possessed excellent banners, flags, bells, and battle-axes;
they held great nooses raised in their hands, as well as clubs;
some had pillars in their hands, others swords, and some wore crowns with serpents rising from them.
Wearing armlets of great serpents and bearing variegated ornaments,
they were all covered in dust and smeared with mud, yet clad in white garments and garlands;
their eyes were formidable, and likewise, they possessed hundreds of faces that shone brilliantly at once.
With blue limbs and lotus-like bodies, and likewise with shaven faces,
those attendants, radiant as gold, joyfully played kettledrums, conchs, clay drums, jharjharas, ānakas, and gomukhas.
Some were singing, while others were dancing;
those of great strength were leaping, bounding, and vaulting. Running with speed and ferocity, their hair was tossed upward by the wind.
Like great elephants in rut, they roared again and again; most terrifying and of fearsome appearance, with spears and sharp-edged axes in their hands,
they were dressed in garments of various colors and adorned with variegated garlands and unguents.
Wearing armlets variegated with jewels, with hands raised aloft,
they were heroes who slew their enemies, possessing an irresistible prowess that was difficult to withstand; they were drinkers of blood and fat, and made their meals of flesh and entrails.
Some had protruding crests and others had ears like lotus-buds; some were emaciated with pot-bellies, while others were extremely short, extremely tall, powerful, or most terrifying.
Some were misshapen with long, dark lips, and others had massive penises and bony calves.
Some wear costly crowns of various kinds, while others are shaven-headed or have matted hair;
they are capable of bringing the heavens, with its sun, moon, planets, and stars, down to the surface of the earth,
and they would venture to destroy the fourfold host of living beings.
And those who are eternally free from fear, the warriors amidst Hara’s frowns,
who act according to their own will, perfected beings, lords of the lords of the three worlds,
ever-delighted by eternal bliss, masters of speech, and devoid of envy.
Those who, having attained the eightfold sovereignty, do not fall into wonder,
and before whose deeds the Blessed Lord Hara is constantly amazed;
and those by whom He is perpetually propitiated with devotion through mind, speech, and action.
10,007.042c With their thoughts, words, and deeds, they protect their devotees like their own biological sons.
10,007.043a Others, however, are always enraged and drink the blood and fat of those who hate the Brahmins;
and they constantly drink the twenty-four-fold Soma.
By means of sacred learning, celibacy, austerity, and self-restraint,
those who have propitiated the trident-marked Lord Maheśvara together with Pārvatī— having become one with his own self— have attained union with Bhava.
The lord of the past, the future, and the present, together with the hosts of spirits, devours them all.
Making the entire universe resound with various and manifold laughter, shouts of joy, cries, and roars, they approached Aśvatthāman.
Praising Mahādeva, emitting light with their great splendor,
they sought to magnify the majesty of the high-souled son of Droṇa;
they desired to test his energy and were eager to behold the slaughter during the night.
Holding in their hands terrible, fierce iron clubs, firebrands, tridents,
and spears, hosts of beings of horrific form gathered from all sides—
beings who would inspire terror even upon the mere sight of them, even for the three worlds.
Even while watching them, the one of great strength felt no distress.
Then the son of Droṇa, bow in hand and with his leather finger-guards bound,
offered himself as a sacrifice by his own self.
In that ritual act, O Bhārata, ten thousand bows were the fuel, the sharpened arrows were the purifiers, and the self of that self-possessed man was the oblation. Then,
with a gentle mantra, the powerful son of Droṇa—

Then, filled with great fury, he offered himself as a sacrifice. Having praised that high-souled Rudra— the unshakable one whose deeds are fierce because of his fierce actions— he spoke thus with palms joined in reverence:

"O Blessed One, today I offer this self, born in the lineage of Aṅgiras, as an oblation into the fire; please accept me as your offering. O Mahādeva, through devotion to you and with supreme concentration."
In this calamity, O Soul of All, I offer myself before you. In you indeed abide all beings, and you abide within all beings;
for the unity of the primary qualities resides in you alone.
"O All-pervading Lord, you who dwell within the hearts of all beings, the sacrificial offering has been presented;
accept me, O God, if my enemies cannot be overcome by me.
Having spoken thus, the son of Droṇa ascended that altar blazing with fire.
Having renounced his very self, he ascended and sat down upon the path of smoke. Seeing him standing there with arms raised, motionless, like an oblation presented,
the Blessed Lord Mahādeva himself spoke as if smiling:
Through truth, purity, uprightness, renunciation, austerity, and self-restraint;
through patience, devotion, fortitude, intellect, and likewise through speech—
I have been duly propitiated by Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds.
Therefore, no one else is dearer to me than Kṛṣṇa.
While honoring him and desiring to test you,
I suddenly protected the Pāñcālas and employed many illusions.
"This honor was rendered to them by me while protecting the Pāñcālas;
yet, overcome by Time, they have no life remaining today.
Having spoken thus to the great archer, the Blessed One [withdrew] his own body.
He entered him and bestowed upon him an excellent, stainless sword.
Then, possessed by the Blessed One, he blazed forth again with splendor;
and through that divinely created energy, he became massive in stature for the battle.
Invisible beings and *rakṣasas* rushed toward him as he proceeded toward the enemy camp like the Lord himself in person—
that great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, as he advanced.
He who, filled with devotion, hears this hymn and recites it to Hara, Sthāṇu, the God of gods,
becomes purified of all sins and goes to the world of Rudra.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When the great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, had thus departed for the camp,
did Kṛpa and the Bhoja not turn back, overcome by fear?
I hope those two great chariot-warriors were not obstructed by lowly guards, nor did they turn back thinking it was impossible;
I hope they have ravaged the camp and slain the Somakas and Pāṇḍavas.
O Saṃjaya, was that vow made by them fruitful during that night? Having reached the ultimate path of Duryodhana in battle,
were they slain by his forces, or did they perhaps not fall upon the earth?
Having performed a most difficult feat, that son of Droṇa now stands there; indeed,
the earth is covered with the slain and sleeping soldiers of the Pāṇḍavas, along with Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, and the sons of Draupadī.
"Or were they slain by the Pañcālas? I hope they did not sleep upon the earth.
Tell me, Sañjaya, what deed was performed by those two.
Sañjaya said:
When that high-souled son of Droṇa had departed for the camp,
Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman stood at the entrance of the camp.
But Aśvatthāman, seeing those two great car-warriors exerting themselves, [remained there].
Greatly delighted, O King, he slowly spoke these words:
"You two are fully capable of destroying the entire kshatriya host;
how much more so this remnant of warriors, especially while they are fast asleep?"
"I shall enter the camp and move about as if it were my time;
you two must act in such a way that not a single man escapes from me alive— this is my firm resolve."
Having spoken thus, the son of Droṇa entered the great camp of the Pārthas,
leaping in through a non-gate, casting aside all fear for himself.
Having entered, the mighty-armed one, being familiar with its layout, [proceeded].
The son of Droṇa, supremely enraged and as if blazing with splendor,
then moved about the entire camp where the people were fast asleep at night;
he approached the dwelling of Dhṛṣṭadyumna slowly.
Having performed great deeds in battle, they were exhausted and fell fast asleep, full of confidence and surrounded by their own troops. Then,
O Bhārata, [Aśvatthāman] entered that dwelling of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
From nearby, the son of Droṇa saw the prince of Pañcāla sleeping on his bed—
a large bed covered with a magnificent white linen cloth,
adorned with excellent garlands and perfumed with incense and aromatic powders.

O lord of the earth, he woke with his foot that high-souled one who was lying down, confident and fearless upon his bed. Having felt the touch of the foot, he rose up, intoxicated by the pride of battle.
The immeasurable-souled one recognized the great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa.
As he was springing up from his bed, the mighty Aśvatthāman seized him by the hair with both hands and crushed him against the surface of the earth.
O Bhārata, crushed by him with force, and overcome by terror and sleep, the Pāñcālya was then unable to move. Having thus crushed the Pāñcālya upon the ground with his might, the son of Droṇa—
Quickly unstringing the bowstring, the cruel-minded and impatient son of Droṇa, frantic with rage, swiftly bound it around his throat; then,
having set his mind on cruelty, he slew the Pāñcālya prince.
O King, having then seized him by both the throat and the chest,
he killed him by strangulation as one slaughters an animal— though he was struggling and crying out—
even as that powerful man was being forcibly restrained by another powerful man with speed.
Scratching the son of Droṇa with his claws, he spoke these words, though not very clearly:
"O son of the preceptor, slay me with a weapon; do not delay!
Having spoken these words, the scorcher of foes fell silent.

"O best of men, the son of the Pāñcāla king has been violently assailed by this powerful one; for your sake, may I go to the worlds of the righteous. Having heard those indistinct words of his, the son of Droṇa replied:
"O defiler of your lineage, there are no worlds for those who slay their preceptor.
My father was killed by you, a cruel man of excessive transgression;
therefore, you too deserve to be slain, O cruel doer of cruelty."
"Therefore, O evil-minded one, you do not deserve death by the sword.
Speaking thus to that hero, the enraged lion struck him in his vital organs with extremely terrible kicks of his hind legs, like a lion attacking an elephant in rut.
By the sound of that hero being slain within the house,
O great king, his wives and those who were his guards were awakened.
Upon seeing him, so tall of stature and possessed of superhuman prowess, they [were struck with wonder].
Determined that he was truly dead, they did not speak out of fear.
Having sent him to the abode of Yama by that means,
the radiant hero reached his beautiful chariot and took his place upon it.
O King, having emerged from his palace and filling the quarters with the sound of his chariot, that mighty warrior set out for the camp, desiring to slay his enemies. Then,
when that great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, had departed, [the battle resumed].
Then, together with all those guards, the women wailed aloud;
seeing the king slain, they were utterly overcome by grief. O Bhārata, all the Kṣatriyas cried out against Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
At that sound, those bulls among Kṣatriyas nearby quickly armed themselves and asked, "What is this?
But the women, O King, were terrified upon seeing that son of Bharadvāja.
With distressed voices, they cried out, "Run quickly!
Whether he be a Rākṣasa or a human, we do not know him who stands upon his chariot after having slain the King of the Pañcālas."
Then those chief warriors suddenly surrounded him;
he struck down all of them as they rushed forward with the Rudra weapon. Having slain Dhṛṣṭadyumna, he likewise destroyed his followers.
He saw Uttamaujas sleeping nearby upon his bed;
attacking him as well with his foot upon the throat and chest by force,
he likewise killed that subduer of enemies as he cried out.
But Yudhāmanyu, arriving there and believing him to have been slain by the Rākṣasa,
raised his mace with force and struck Drona’s son in the chest.
Struck by that blow from the mace, Drona’s son did not tremble in the battle.
Rushing toward him, he seized him and threw him down upon the earth; and as he writhed like a beast, he likewise slew him. Having thus slain him, that hero then rushed against others.
O Indra among kings, having attacked the Pāñcāla heroes who were fast asleep here and there, the enraged [Kṛṣṇa] slew those great car-warriors nearby,
as they were quivering and trembling like sacrificial animals being slaughtered at a sacrifice.
Then, taking up his sword,

he who was skilled in sword-fighting struck down other common folk as he moved through the various paths; likewise, he beheld those stationed in the military outposts lying asleep within the encampments.
In an instant, he struck down all those who were exhausted and had laid aside their weapons;
with his excellent sword, he cut through warriors, horses, and elephants,
his entire body drenched in blood like the Destroyer unleashed by Time.
With those quivering [weapons], with the raising of his sword, and likewise with its brandishing, the son of Droṇa was drenched in blood in three ways. As he fought,
drenched in blood and wielding his blazing sword, [he appeared like a mountain].
His form appeared superhuman and most terrifying.
O Kauravya, even those who were awake were bewildered by that sound;
looking at one another and beholding the son of Droṇa, they trembled with fear.
Seeing that form of his, those kṣatriyas, the destroyers of their enemies, thinking him to be a rākṣasa, closed their eyes. Then,
assuming a terrible form, he roamed through the camp like Time itself.
He beheld the sons of Draupadī and the remaining Somakas. Terrified by that sound, O lord of the people, those great car-warriors, with bows in hand,
heard that Dhṛṣṭadyumna had been slain and [saw] the sons of Draupadī.
Fearlessly, they overwhelmed the son of Bharadvāja with showers of arrows.
Then, awakened by that roar, the Prabhadrakas and Śikhaṇḍin assailed the son of Droṇa with stone-tipped shafts.
But Bhāradvāja, seeing them raining down showers of arrows,
let out a powerful roar, desiring to slay those who were so difficult to conquer.
Then, remembering the slaughter of his father, he became exceedingly enraged.
Descending from the seat of his chariot, he rushed forward in haste,
seizing in that battle a massive shield adorned with a thousand moons and a vast,
divine sword embellished with gold.
10,008.049e Having rushed toward the sons of Draupadī, the powerful one moved about with his sword.
10,008.050a Then, O King, that tiger among men struck Prativindhya in the region of the belly during that battle; being slain, he fell to the earth.
Having pierced the son of Droṇa with a lance, the powerful Sutasoma again raised his sword and rushed toward Drona’s son. But then,
in that battle, the son of Droṇa warded off the blow of the lance.

Having severed Sutasoma’s arm along with his sword, that bull among men struck him again in the side; with his heart pierced, he fell. But the valiant Śatānīka, son of Nakula, [struck] with a chariot wheel.
Lifting him up with both arms, he struck him violently in the chest;
that twice-born one then struck Śatānīka as he released his discus. Rendered unconscious, he fell to the ground, and then [the other] struck off his head.
Śrutakarman, seizing a club,
rushed toward the son of Droṇa and struck him violently on his left cheek.
But he [Aśvatthāman] struck Śrutakarman in the face with an excellent sword.
Struck down, he fell to the ground, unconscious and with a distorted face.
At that sound, however, the heroic Śrutakīrti, wielder of the great bow,
approached Aśvatthāman and overwhelmed him with a shower of arrows.
O great king, the great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, was seen covered by those arrows as if he were a porcupine bristling with its quills; yet he,
having warded off his showers of arrows with his shield, [continued on].
With his earrings, he struck off from the body that radiant head.
Then the powerful slayer of Bhīṣma, together with all the Prabhadrakas,
struck that hero from every side with various weapons.
With another stone-tipped arrow, he also struck him between the eyebrows.
But the mighty son of Droṇa, overcome with rage,
approached Śikhaṇḍin and cut him in two with his sword.
Then, having slain Śikhaṇḍin, that scorcher of foes, overcome with rage,
rushed impetuously against all the hosts of the Prabhadrakas and also against whatever force of Virāṭa remained.
Seeing them again and again, the one of great strength wrought a terrible slaughter among the sons, grandsons, and friends of Drupada,
repeatedly charging against various men one after another.
The son of Droṇa, skilled in the maneuvers of the sword, cut down with his blade a single female figure—
Kālī— who had a red mouth and eyes, was adorned with red garlands and unguents,
wore red garments, held a noose in her hand, and possessed a crest of hair.
They beheld Kālarātri standing there with a smile,
having set out while binding men, horses, and elephants with terrible nooses;
and likewise, O great king, they saw the great chariot-warriors who had laid down their weapons.

On other nights, O noble one, those leaders of warriors saw her in their dreams leading away various departed spirits— bound by nooses and with disheveled hair— as she carried them off while they slept; and they saw the son of Droṇa constantly slaying them.

From the moment the battle between the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas began, they saw that magical creation (kṛtyā) and the son of Droṇa (Drauṇi) from that point onward. It was the son of Droṇa who, after they had already been struck down by fate, laid them low.
Terrifying all beings with his terrifying roars,
he was remembered by those heroes; though oppressed by fate, they thought, "This is that very sight from former times."
Then, by that roar, the archers in the camp of the Pāṇḍavas were awakened by the hundreds and thousands;
he cut off the feet of one and the hips of another.
Like the Destroyer unleashed by Time, he pierced some on their flanks;
O Lord, the earth became strewn with elephants and horses crushed to death, some violently mangled, others screaming in extreme agony.
"Crying out, 'What is this? Who is this? What is this sound?
What has been done?', so did the son of Droṇa then become like Death to them.
[He struck] the Pāṇḍus and Sṛñjayas, who were frantic and deprived of their weapons and armor."
Drauni, the best among strikers, dispatched them to the world of death. Then, terrified by those weapons, leaping up in the grip of fear,
blinded by sleep and deprived of their senses, they hid here and there.
Seized by stiffness of the thighs and their vigor struck down by dejection,
they cried out in great terror and crushed one another.
Then the son of Droṇa once again mounted his chariot, which resounded with a terrible roar.
With bow in hand, he dispatched others with his arrows to the abode of Yama;
some of those best of men who were leaping up from afar,
and other heroes who were rushing forward, he offered up to the Night of Doom.
In that very manner, he rushed forward, crushing [the enemy] with the front of his chariot;
then he rained down various showers of arrows upon the foes. And again, with a most variegated shield adorned with a hundred moons—
With that sword, which had the color of the sky,
the son of Droṇa, intoxicated by battle, then agitated their camp,
O king of kings, like an elephant agitating a great lake.
O King, at that sound, the warriors rose up bewildered;
afflicted by sleep and overcome by fear, they fled hither and thither,
while others cried out with many kinds of loud lamentations.
Others shrieked discordantly and spoke much that was incoherent; they could no longer grasp their weapons or their garments. Others, with their hair disheveled, could no longer recognize one another.
Some enemies, terrified, leapt up; others there wandered about aimlessly.
Some discharged excrement, and some passed urine.
And, O king of kings, the horses and elephants broke their bonds.
Others flew about together, creating a great commotion;
some men there, overcome by fear, hid themselves in the earth,
while elephants and horses trampled those who had fallen in that very manner.
While that was occurring, O bull among men, the *rākṣasas*,
being satiated, roared loudly with joy, O best of the Bharatas. That sound, O King, was set forth by the hosts of beings filled with delight.
That great roar filled all the directions as well as the heavens. Hearing their cries of distress, O King, the terrified elephants and horses bolted loose and fled, trampling the people in the camp.
By the dust raised by their feet as they ran about there,
a darkness twice as thick as the night was created within their camp.
When that darkness had arisen, the people everywhere became utterly bewildered.

O Bhārata, fathers did not recognize their sons, nor brothers their own brothers; elephants, deprived of riders, trampled other elephants, and horses likewise struck down, broke, and crushed other horses.
Broken, falling, and striking one another, they felled their enemies and,
having felled them, crushed them as well;
for the men were senseless, overcome by sleep, and enveloped in darkness.
Driven on by Time, they then began to slaughter their own people there; abandoning the gates, the gatekeepers, as well as the outposts and the sentries,
fled to the best of their ability, bewildered and not knowing where to go.
And having become utterly lost to one another, O Lord, they did not recognize each other then;
with their minds struck by fate, they cried out, "O father! O son!
as they fled in all directions, abandoning even their own kinsmen.
Then those people, calling out to one another by their lineages and names, lay prostrate upon the earth while crying out "Alas! Alas!
Perceiving them, that son of Droṇa, intoxicated by battle, slaughtered them.
There, others, being struck again and again, senseless and oppressed by fear, fled from their camps; those Kṣatriyas,
terrified and desiring to live, rushed out from the encampments.
Kṛtavarman and Kṛpa struck down at the gateway those who were without weapons,
machines, or armor, with disheveled hair and palms joined in supplication;
trembling on the ground in fear, they did not release anyone at all.
Not one of those two emerged from the camp;
O great king, neither Kṛpa nor the evil-minded son of Hṛdika was released.
Furthermore, those two desired to do what was pleasing to the son of Droṇa.
In three locations, they set fire to Śibi’s camp.
Then, O great king, while the camp was illuminated, Aśvatthāman, the delighter of his father, moved about with his sword like one of practiced hand.
With his sword, that best of the twice-born deprived some heroes of their lives as they were charging at him, and others as they were fleeing; that valiant one,
having sliced some warriors in two with his sword in the midst of the fray.
The son of Droṇa, filled with fury, struck them down like stalks of sesame,
O bull of the Bharatas; the earth became strewn with the fallen remains of the best of men, horses, and elephants, who were screaming in extreme agony.
When thousands of men had been slain and fallen,
many headless trunks (kabandhas) rose up and, having risen, fell down again;
he lopped off arms still clutching weapons and adorned with armlets, as well as heads.
O Bhārata, having encountered those whose thighs were like the trunks of elephants, as well as their hands and feet,
the son of Droṇa cut off the backs of some, severed the heads of others, likewise cut through the sides of others, and even turned some away from the fight.
He cut some men at the waist, others at the ears,
and striking others at the shoulders, he drove their heads into their chests.
As he moved about in this manner, slaughtering a great many men, [the battle raged on].
The night, shrouded in darkness, appeared terrible and fearsome to behold;
with thousands of men slain and their lives taken,
and with many elephants and horses, the earth became a sight of horror.
In that place crowded with Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, and made terrible by chariots, horses, and elephants,
[the warriors], cut down by the enraged son of Droṇa, fell to the earth;
some cried out for their mothers, others for their fathers, and others for their brothers.
Some said: "That which was done to us while we were fast asleep by the Rākṣasas of cruel deeds was not done in battle by the enraged sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
for it was due to the absence of the Pārthas that this slaughter was wrought upon us."
The son of Kuntī, who has Janārdana as his protector, cannot be conquered by gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, or rākṣasas—
he who is devoted to Brahman, truthful in speech, self-controlled, and compassionate toward all beings.

Dhananjaya, the son of Pṛthā, does not slay one who is asleep, nor one who is intoxicated, nor one who has laid down his weapons, nor one with palms joined in reverence, nor one who is running away, nor one with disheveled hair. Yet this terrible deed has been committed against us by Rākṣasas of cruel deeds.
"Thus many people lay there lamenting;
and while some men were groaning and others were moaning,
that great and tumultuous noise subsided after a moment."
O lord of the earth, as the ground was drenched with blood,
that tumultuous and terrible dust vanished in an instant. Thousands [of warriors], being overwhelmed, agitated, and devoid of energy, [lay there].
Enraged, he struck down men like Paśupati striking down beasts;
the son of Droṇa crushed all— those lying there embracing one another, those fleeing, those cowering, and those still fighting.
Being scorched by the fire and slaughtered by him, those warriors then sent one another to the abode of Yama. By the end of that night, however, the great army of the Pāṇḍavas—
O Indra among kings, the son of Droṇa sent them to the abode of Yama.
That night, which increased the joy of the night-roaming creatures,
was exceedingly fierce and destructive of men, elephants, and horses.
There, various kinds of *rakṣas* and *piśācas* were seen,
devouring human flesh and drinking blood—
fearsome, tawny, and fierce, with teeth like crags and covered in dust.
They had matted hair, long thighs, five feet, and large bellies; they had fingers on their backs, were coarse, deformed, and possessed terrifying voices;
they had knees like jars, were extremely short, blue-throated, and fearsome.
Accompanied by their sons and wives, those exceedingly cruel, hideous,
and pitiless beings were seen there in various forms;
and others, having drunk blood, danced joyfully in groups.
"This is excellent, this is pure, this is delicious," they cried out. Greedily devouring the fat, marrow, bones, blood,
and adipose tissues, those flesh-eaters who subsist on meat consumed the finest human flesh.
Others, having drunk fat, ran about with distended bellies;
likewise there were fierce flesh-eaters and consumers of raw meat with various faces.
There were tens of thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions of them there.
O lord of men, at that great slaughter, many beings of terrible form— mighty rākṣasas of cruel deeds who were joyful and satiated—
had assembled there.
At the hour of dawn, he desired to depart from the camp.
O Lord, the sword with its dark hilt, which had been drenched in human blood,
seemed to have become one with the hand that grasped it.
Having left no enemies remaining in that slaughter of men,
he shone resplendent like the fire at the end of a Yuga after it has reduced all beings to ashes.
O Lord, having thus accomplished that deed according to his vow, the son of Droṇa—
Having cleared the difficult path for his father, he was freed from his fever;
just as he had entered the camp at night while the people were fast asleep,
even so did that bull among men depart silently after having struck them down.
Having emerged from that camp and met with those two,
the valiant one, being joyful, related all that deed to them, O Lord, while gladdening them;
and they too, acting for his pleasure, then told him the pleasant news.
The Pāñcālas and Sṛñjayas were being slaughtered by the thousands;
they shouted loudly with joy and likewise slapped their palms.
Indeed, such was that night during the destruction of the Somakas.
While they were fast asleep and heedless, there occurred an exceedingly terrible slaughter;
for undoubtedly the turn of time is difficult to overcome,
since such men as those were slain there, having caused the destruction of our people.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Why did that great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, who was intent on the victory of my son, not perform such a mighty deed even earlier?
"Why then, when the kṣatriyas had been slain, did that son of Droṇa, the great archer, perform this deed? You ought to explain that to me.
Saṃjaya said:
Surely, out of fear of them, O joy of the Kurus, he did not do this;
for it was accomplished by the son of Droṇa due to the absence of the sons of Pṛthā, the wise Keśava,
and even Sātyaki.
"Even the Lord of the Maruts could not have slain them in their presence;
such was the conduct, O King, while the people were asleep, O Lord.
Then, having caused that great calamity and the destruction of the people among the Pāṇḍavas,"

"By good fortune! By good fortune! the great chariot-warriors said to one another as they met. Then the son of Droṇa embraced them both, who greeted him in return; and out of joy, he spoke these most excellent words: 10,008.148e "By good fortune! By good fortune! the great chariot-warriors said to one another as they met. 10,008.149a Then the son of Droṇa embraced them, and was greeted by them in return. 10,008.149c And out of joy, he uttered this most magnificent speech.

All the Pāñcālas have been slain, as have all the sons of Draupadī; the Somakas and the remnants of the Matsyas have all been destroyed by me. Now we have accomplished our purpose; let us go there without delay.
"If the king still lives, we shall tell him this pleasant news.
Sañjaya said:
"Having slain all the Pāñcālas and all the sons of Draupadī, they—"
They went together to the place where Duryodhana had been slain.
Having arrived, they saw that the lord of men still possessed some breath of life;
then, leaping down from their chariots, they surrounded your son.

O Indra among kings, they beheld him upon the surface of the earth with his thigh shattered, his life-breath ebbing away, and deprived of consciousness; he was vomiting blood from his mouth and was surrounded on all sides by many beasts of prey of terrifying appearance.
And seeing him being devoured from close at hand by packs of jackals,
he was with great difficulty warding off those beasts of prey eager to devour him,
while he writhed upon the ground in intense and agonizing pain.
The three surviving heroes— Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata— stood around that high-souled one as he lay upon the ground, drenched in his own blood, afflicted with grief.
Surrounded by those three great car-warriors, sighing and smeared with blood,
the king shone like a sacrificial altar surrounded by the three fires.
Beholding the king lying there in such an unaccustomed state, they gazed upon him.
Shedding tears from their grief and sighing deeply, O King,
those three princes were then overcome by unbearable sorrow and wept aloud.
Then, with their hands, they wiped the blood from his face.
10,009.009c As the king lay there on the battlefield, they lamented piteously. 10,009.010 Kṛpa said:
10,009.010a "There is no burden too great for destiny, since he here is drenched in blood."
Duryodhana, the lord of eleven armies, lies slain.
Behold this mace, adorned with gold,
fallen upon the ground beside him who was so fond of the mace and possessed a complexion like gold.
This mace does not leave this hero in battle after battle;
indeed, it does not abandon the illustrious one even as he departs for heaven.
Behold it here together with the hero, adorned with gold.
He who was the scorcher of foes, who indeed went at the head of those consecrated with the *mūrdhāvasikta* rite, now lies upon his bed like a devoted wife, as if full of affection;
slain, he devours the dust— behold the reversal of time!
By whom his enemies were formerly struck down in battle and lay upon the earth—
that very Kuru king now lies slain on the ground by his foes,
he before whom hundreds of kings used to bow in fear.
He lies upon the bed of heroes, surrounded by flesh-eating beasts.
Those kings who formerly waited upon him as their lord for the sake of wealth—fie on him! Slain this very day, he now lies there; behold the reversal of Time.
Today, deer and jackals indeed wait upon him in the forest;
today, flesh-eaters, greedy for meat, attend to him. Today, those who crave flesh, O Kauravya, wait upon that descendant of Kuru.
10,009.018 Saṃjaya said: Then, O best of the Bharatas, having beheld that foremost of kings lying there, Aśvatthāman lamented piteously.
"O tiger among kings, they say that you are the foremost of all archers,
equal to the Lord of Wealth himself in battle, and the disciple of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
O sinless one, how did Bhīmasena find an opening against you?"
"O King, though he was always powerful and skillful, that evil-minded one has been slain;
O Great King, Time is surely the most powerful force in this world,
since we behold you struck down by Bhīmasena in battle."
"How could the base and wicked Vṛkodara, that fool, have slain you— who know all dharmas— through deceit? Surely time is difficult to overcome,
for he challenged you to battle with his might in an unrighteous manner."
When your thighs were shattered by Bhīmasena with his mace, and you were slain unrighteously in battle, that base Yudhiṣṭhira looked on as your head was being trampled underfoot; fie upon him!
"Shame on that wicked man who speaks falsely of his righteousness!
This evil deed which Bhīmasena has committed through deceit—
the warriors will surely censure Vṛkodara in battles."
"As long as living beings shall endure, you have indeed been struck down by deceit.
O King, did not the heroic Rāma, the joy of the Yadus, always say of you:
'There is no one equal to Duryodhana with the mace'?"
"O King, descendant of Bharata, the Vārṣṇeya indeed praises you in assemblies,
saying, 'The Kauravya is my excellent pupil in the art of mace-fighting,' O Lord.
This is the goal that the supreme ṛṣis declare to be the most praiseworthy for a kṣatriya."
"O Duryodhana, bull among men, I do not grieve for you who have been slain in battle while facing your foe;
rather, I grieve for Gāndhārī and for your father, whose sons have been killed."
"O Hero, since we have been rendered protectorless by you, our protector, while being slain,
these two beggars shall wander this earth in grief. Fie upon Kṛṣṇa the Vārṣṇeya, and also upon the evil-minded Arjuna!"
Those two who consider themselves knowers of dharma yet looked on with indifference while you were being slain—
what will all those Pāṇḍavas say to the lords of men? How can they, shameless as they are, explain how Duryodhana was killed by us?

"O son of Gandhārī, you are fortunate, for you have been slain in battle while facing the enemies, O bull among men, according to the dharma. For Gandhārī herself has had her sons killed, and her kinsmen and relatives slaughtered."
And the invincible one, whose eye is wisdom— what destiny will he attain? Fie upon Kṛtavarman, upon me, and upon the great car-warrior Kṛpa,
we who have not gone to heaven while placing you, O king, at our head!
"You are the giver of all desires, the protector, and the benefactor of your subjects;
