since we do not follow you, shame on us, the lowest of men!
By your heroic power, as well as that of Kṛpa and my own father—"

O tiger among men, by your grace, we— along with our friends and kinsmen— have obtained houses filled with jewels and have performed many preeminent sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
"And from where shall we obtain such a caravan as that with which you have gone forth, placing yourself at its head above all kings? O King,
we three alone shall go along as you proceed toward the supreme goal."
"Indeed, we shall suffer because we do not follow you;
deprived of you and heaven, our purpose lost, we shall remember your virtuous deeds.
What indeed could that action be by which we might truly follow after you?"
"O best of the Kurus, we shall surely wander this earth in misery;
O King, deprived of you, where can there be peace for us, and where can there be happiness? Having gone there, O Great King, you must meet these great chariot-warriors."
"O lord of men, at my word, you must honor them according to their excellence and seniority;
having honored the preceptor, the banner of all archers,
report that Dhrishtadyumna has been slain by me today."
You should embrace King Bāhlīka, that great chariot-warrior, as well as the ruler of the Sindhus, Somadatta, and Bhūriśravas; likewise,
those other best of kings who have already gone to heaven.
"From our words, you should embrace him and inquire after his well-being.
Having spoken thus to the king, who was broken-thighed and unconscious,
Aśvatthāman looked at him and spoke these words again.
"O Duryodhana, if you still live, listen to these words that are pleasant to the ear:
seven remain from the side of the Pāṇḍavas, and three of us from the side of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons— namely,
those five brothers, Vāsudeva, and Sātyaki."
I, Kṛtavarman, and Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat,
as well as all the sons of Draupadī and the sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, have been slain;
all the Pāñcālas have been killed, O Bhārata, and only a remnant of the Matsyas remains.
"Behold the retaliation for what was done; for the sons of Pāṇḍu have been slain.
During the night-attack, their camp was destroyed along with its men and mounts. And that evildoer Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O lord of the earth, has been slain by me."
Having entered the camp at night, he was killed like an animal.
But Duryodhana, having heard those words so dear to his heart,
regained his composure and spoke these words again:
Neither the son of Gaṅgā, nor Karṇa, nor your father did for me what has been done by you today, joined with Kṛpa and the Bhoja;
for that base commander has been slain along with Śikhaṇḍin.
"Therefore, I consider myself today indeed equal to Maghavan.
May you attain well-being; may blessings be upon you. May we meet again in heaven.
Having spoken thus, the high-minded king of the Kurus became silent.
When his life-breaths had been released according to the natural law and had ascended into the sky,
Kṛpā and the others, filled with wonder, departed like flashes of lightning. His holy body ascended to heaven, while his physical frame remained upon the earth.
"O King, thus has your son Duryodhana met his end;
that hero, having gone to the forefront of the battle, was subsequently slain by his enemies. That brave man gave up his life, casting grief upon his friends."
Saying "So be it," they embraced him, and having embraced that king,
they beheld Suyodhana situated in a celestial chariot in the sky,
surrounded by hosts of Indra’s attendants and adorned with divine garlands and unguents.
Saying "Excellent! Excellent! again and again, and repeatedly looking upon him with compassion and other [virtues], they mounted their own chariots. Having thus heard these piteous words of your son—
At the hour of dawn, afflicted with grief, I ran toward the city. Thus, O King, did this terrible, slaughtering, and fierce destruction of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies occur through your evil counsel.
"O sinless one, now that your son has gone to heaven, my divine vision granted by the ṛṣis has indeed vanished today for me who am afflicted with grief.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus heard of the slaughter of his sons and kinsmen, the king then sighed long and hot, and thereafter became lost in thought. Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men...
[Having recited] the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the Jaya.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When that night had passed, Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s charioteer...
He reported to Dharmarāja the slaughter committed during the night attack;
O Great King, the sons of Draupadī, together with the sons of Drupada,
were sleeping heedlessly and trustfully in their own camp at night.
"Your camp was destroyed at night by the cruel Kṛtavarman, by Kṛpa the son of Gotama, and by the wicked Aśvatthāman— these men having slain your men,
elephants, and horses with spears, javelins, and battle-axes."
Ten thousand [of them], cutting him down, have left your army without remainder;
it was like a vast forest, bent low by the weight of various birds and fruits, being felled by axes.
O Bhārata, a very great clamor from your army was heard;
O lord of the earth, I alone remained from that host,
having somehow escaped while Kṛtavarman was preoccupied, O virtuous-souled one.

Having heard those inauspicious words, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī— though difficult to overcome— fell to the earth, overwhelmed by grief for his sons. As he was falling, Sātyaki stepped forward and caught him.
Bhimasena, Arjuna, and the two sons of Madri— all the Pandavas— were there.
But the son of Kunti, having regained consciousness, lamented in distress with a voice overwhelmed by grief,
crying out as one who, though having conquered his enemies, was himself finally conquered.
The course of events is difficult to discern, even for those who possess divine vision.
Others, while being defeated, conquer; we, though victorious, are defeated. Having slain our brothers, friends, fathers, sons, and circles of well-wishers, [we remain].

Having conquered our kinsmen, ministers, and grandsons, we have all been defeated. For that which appears to be gain is actually loss, and likewise, that which appears to be loss is actually gain. This victory has the appearance of defeat; therefore, this victory is truly a defeat.
Having conquered whom one later suffers, like a fool who has met with calamity—
how could he consider that a victory when he is more thoroughly defeated by his enemies than they were?
For the sake of whose wealth this sinful victory was achieved through the slaughter of friends— fie upon that victory!
For by those who are vigilant and have conquered themselves, those who appear victorious are truly defeated.
[They were defeated] in battle by that fierce one whose tusks were barbed and reed-arrows, whose tongue was the sword,
whose gaping mouth was the bow, and who roared with the sound of the bowstring striking his palm.
These men, who were spared by Karna when he was enraged— that lion among men who never fled in battles— have now been slain through his negligence.
[They fell into] that lake of chariots, surging with waves of showers of arrows.
It was strewn with jewels and possessed rows of vehicles;
it had spears, swords, fish-emblems, banners, serpents, and crocodiles as its aquatic creatures;
it had bows for its whirlpools and great arrows for its foam.
Those who crossed the ocean of Droṇa— the tide of whose surging speed was the rising moon of battle, and whose roar was the sound of bowstrings and wheel-rims—
by means of the various ships that were their weapons;
Those princes were slain through negligence;
for there is nothing superior to negligence as a cause of death for men in this world of the living.
For wealth abandons a man from all sides when he is heedless,
and misfortunes enter him;
[he is like] one with a smoke-banner raised at the very peak of his excellent standard.
With arrows for its flames and the great wind of his anger,
with the roar of his great bowstring, palms, and wheel-rims,
he performed a sacrifice of various armors and weapons.
Those who withstood the great forest fire that was Bhīṣma in the great battle— him who was assailed by the best of the great armies,
and whose force of weapons was grasped and extended.
Those princes were slain through negligence;
for knowledge, austerity, prosperity, or vast fame cannot be attained by a man who is negligent.
Behold, having slain all enemies through vigilance, Mahendra prospers in happiness,
along with the sons and grandsons of kings who are equal to Indra.
Behold how those who have crossed the ocean, prosperous merchants, have been destroyed without distinction through negligence,
like those who, having reached a shallow stream, perish by disregarding it.
Those who were slain while lying down by those filled with indignation have, without doubt, attained the third heaven.
But I grieve for the virtuous Kṛṣṇā; how will she fare?
Having heard that his brothers and sons were slain, as well as the King of the Pāñcālas and his aged father, he will now perish in an ocean of grief.
Surely she has fallen unconscious upon the earth;
with her slender body wasted by grief, she will lie there,
unable to endure that sorrow born of lamentation.
How will she, driven by the loss of her son and the slaughter of her brother, become accustomed to pleasures—
she who is as if being consumed by fire?
Thus lamenting in his distress,
the king of the Kurus spoke to Nakula:
"Go, bring that unfortunate woman here."
Having accepted those words of the king, who was equal to Dharma himself, the son of Mādrī took the princess along with her maternal kin in accordance with righteousness.
He went quickly by chariot to the residence of the queen,
where the wife of the Pāñcāla king was;
having dispatched the son of Mādrī, the descendant of Ajamīḍha—
Afflicted with grief and accompanied by those friends,
he went wailing toward the battlefield of his sons, which was crowded with throngs of spirits.
Having entered that inauspicious place of fierce aspect,
he saw his sons, friends,
and companions lying on the ground, their limbs drenched in blood.
Seeing them with their heads severed, shattered,
or carried away,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the best among the upholders of dharma, was deeply distressed.
The foremost of the Kauravas cried out loudly and fell unconscious upon the earth along with his followers.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having seen his sons, brothers, and friends thus slain in battle,
O Janamejaya, his soul was overwhelmed with great sorrow;
then a vast grief arose within that high-souled one.
As he remembered his sons, grandsons, brothers, and kinsmen,
his eyes became filled with tears; trembling and deprived of his senses,
his friends, deeply distressed, then began to comfort him.
Having performed the funeral rites for all those sons of immeasurable splendor according to the prescribed rules, he became deeply afflicted with grief. Then,
at that very moment at dawn, [he departed] in a chariot radiant as the sun.
At that very moment, Nakula arrived with swift horses adorned with golden garlands, accompanied by Draupadī, who was deeply afflicted.
Having heard that most grievous and unpleasant news while she was at Upaplavya, she had set out.
Then, at the prospect of the destruction of all her sons, she became deeply distressed,
trembling like a plantain tree shaken by the wind;
and Kṛṣṇā, overcome with grief upon reaching the king, fell to the ground.
The face of her, whose eyes were like the petals of a full-blown lotus, suddenly became emaciated by grief, like the sun eclipsed by darkness. Then,
seeing her fallen, he of true prowess was filled with indignation.
Vṛkodara approached and took her by both arms;
comforted by Bhīmasena,
that beautiful lady Kṛṣṇā, weeping, spoke to the Pāṇḍava along with his brother.
"By good fortune, O King, you shall today enjoy this entire earth,
having handed over your sons to Yama according to the duty of a Kṣatriya.
By good fortune, O Pārtha, you are safe, [having reached] that horse which moves like a rutting elephant."
"O King, having bestowed the kingdom upon your younger brothers, depart for the forest with me; O Lord, abandon this painful craving for sovereignty.
Such is the bitter fruit of kingship, whose consequence is so acrid."
Where, having committed the slaughter of kinsmen, one seeks happiness through a kingdom—
for the sake of which that kingdom, enjoyments, wealth, and riches are desired—
they have been slain like cattle by destiny in the form of the son of Droṇa.
"O King, surely your heart is fashioned from diamond;
for thus you always witness the sorrows of me, an unfortunate woman, even while looking upon my lords, who are like the gods and the protectors of the world."
O lord of men, remembering today their happiness and youth,
as well as their various activities appropriate to that stage of life—
how, O Indra among kings, will you be able to live for even a single moment?
"O Indra among kings, my brothers were under your control like servants.
Thinking of them, O King, how will you fare?
O Ruler of the Earth, having relied upon what will you find delight when the time comes?"
For you are indeed deprived of sons and grandsons, as well as sisters' husbands, kinsmen,
relatives who have fulfilled their duties, friends, and likewise paternal relations;
or else, if you are a wretch dwelling in the possession of a kingdom yet still craving enjoyments.
"Let it be as you wish; I shall give up my life.
Prepare a funeral pyre for me quickly, for I shall enter the fire.
You will never carry out this very command of mine."

"O Lord of Men, how could it be right for me to remain alive even for a moment while that evil-doing son of Droṇa lives? I shall give up my life by means of poison, a rope, or by falling [from a height]; as long as he who has committed such wickedness lives, my own life holds no value."
"Right here, O auspicious one, I shall sit in the vow of fasting; spread the darbha grass for me.
How indeed shall I endure this suffering, which is like the fall of a thunderbolt, while crying out 'Alas! Alas! and remembering my sons who have become Tathāgatas?"
Death is in every way better for me than life,
O King, since while my circle of brothers was sleeping at night, my life was snatched away here like that of common cattle. But as for him—
"I shall not sustain my life for even a moment while he lives.
Therefore, I shall abandon my life by resorting to fasting right here before you;
even after you have obtained the entire earth, you will not remember the son of Subhadrā."

Having heard that your heroic sons were struck down by that dharma while they were sleeping with me at Upaplavya, and having heard of the slaughter of those who were fast asleep by the evil-doing son of Droṇa, may it be by good fortune that you do not remember this.
O Pārtha, grief burns me like fire consumes its own bed;
for if today in battle you do not, by displaying your prowess, take the life of that evil-doing son of Droṇa along with his followers.
"Right here I shall sit in fasting unto death; take note of this, O Pāṇḍavas, if the son of Droṇa does not reap the fruit of his sinful deed.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇā then sat down facing the Pāṇḍava.
Seeing Yudhiṣṭhira, the illustrious Dharmarāja, seated, the glorious Yājñasenī sat down; and the righteous Pāṇḍava king, that royal seer, replied to his beloved queen,
the beautiful Draupadī.
"O knower of dharma, O auspicious one, those sons and brothers of yours have met their end in accordance with dharma and by means of dharma; you ought not to grieve for them.
Having heard that, she was overcome with trembling, her anger having been aroused.
"O auspicious one, that son of Droṇa has gone to a forest far from here. O beautiful lady, how will you know of his fall in battle?
Draupadī said:
"I have heard that there is a jewel on the head of Droṇa’s son that was born with him. Having slain that wicked man in battle, I would see that jewel brought back;
O King, my intention is that I might live by placing it upon my own head."
10,011.021 Vaiśampāyana said: Having spoken thus to the Pāṇḍava and the king, the beautiful Kṛṣṇā then approached Bhīmasena and, filled with anger, spoke these words.
"O Bhīma, remembering the duty of a Kṣatriya, you ought to protect me; slay that evildoer Śambara as Maghavan [slays] Śambara. For there is no man here who is equal to you in prowess."
This has been heard throughout all the worlds how, in a time of supreme calamity,
you indeed became an island for the sons of Pṛthā in the city of Vāraṇāvata,
and likewise you were their refuge upon the appearance of Hiḍimbā.
Likewise, in the city of Virāṭa, you rescued me when I was severely oppressed by Kīcaka, just as Maghavan rescued Paulomī from her distress;
for you have indeed performed these great deeds in the past, O Pārtha.
Likewise, O slayer of enemies, having slain the son of Droṇa, be at peace. Drawing your bow with an arrow and swiftly urging on the horses,
O tiger among men, having slain that wicked one, be at peace.
Having heard her various lamentations filled with grief,
the mighty Bhimasena, son of Kuntī, could not endure it;
he mounted his great chariot, its frame adorned with gold.
Taking up his beautiful and variegated bow, equipped with arrows and a string,
and appointing Nakula as his charioteer, he resolved upon the slaughter of Droṇa’s son; drawing that bow with its arrow, he swiftly urged the horses forward.
O tiger among men, those bay horses, swift as the wind and driven on,
moved with great speed;
the ever-victorious one, having taken his chariot from his own camp, followed its tracks.
The valiant one quickly followed the path of Droṇa’s son’s chariot.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When that invincible bull among the Yadus had thus departed, then—
The lotus-eyed one said to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī:
"O Pāṇḍava, this brother of yours, O Bhārata, unable to endure his grief for his son,
goes to the battlefield, O Bhārata, desiring to slay the son of Droṇa."
"O bull of the Bharatas, Bhīma is dearer to you than all your other brothers;
why do you not assist him now that he has fallen into such distress?
Furthermore, hear this supreme secret of mine, and having heard it, act accordingly."

Why will you not support that mighty-armed and immensely powerful Bhīmasena as he advances, seeking to slay the son of Droṇa? For his soul is overwhelmed with wrath, and he has assumed a form like that of Śaṅkara.
The son of Droṇa, who is incapable of being slain by all the worlds and possessed of supreme wrath, will slay that Bhīma— who is overwhelmed by rage and afflicted by the death of his sons—
merely upon seeing him, for he is a hero skilled in great weapons.
"He is a hero and he is valiant; filled with wrath, he will destroy us.
Therefore, O Great King, O bull of the Bharata race, let us march against Bhīma, as Droṇa, the conqueror of enemy cities, told his son."
The weapon named Brahmashiras, which could consume even the entire earth—
that weapon the high-souled and illustrious preceptor, the banner of all archers, being well-pleased, bestowed upon Dhananjaya.
His son, the impatient Aśvatthāman, likewise entreated him in this very manner; then, seeing that Arjuna had acquired the Brahmāśiras weapon, the mighty Aśvatthāman spoke to his own father.
Overcome by great anger upon seeing this reversal of affection, he said:
"O father, why did you not give the Brahmāstra, along with its secret lore— which was bestowed upon Arjuna— to me, your virtuous son?"
O Bhārata, perceiving that he was angry and out of affection for his son,
he then spoke to his son with a heart that was not very joyful,
for the restlessness of his high-souled son was already known to him.
Even though he was a hero of wrathful aspect, a warrior of exceeding indignation,
the preceptor, who knew all duties, did not seek out his son constantly; for even when you had fallen into the greatest calamity in battle, O dear one, he did not [forsake you].
"This weapon must be employed especially against human beings," said the preceptor Droṇa to his son; and having spoken thus, he later added,
"O bull among men, you shall never stand upon the path of the virtuous."
Having understood those unpleasant words of his father, that evil-minded man, despairing of all blessings, wandered the earth lamenting.
Then, O best of the Kurus, descendant of Bharata, while you were dwelling in the forest...
Having arrived at Dvārakā, he dwelt there, highly honored by the Vṛṣṇis. Once, while living near Dvāravatī on the shore of the ocean,
he approached me alone and spoke to me as if smiling.
O Kṛṣṇa, that fierce ascetic power which my father— the preceptor of the Bharatas and one whose prowess is truth— obtained from Agastya,
is the weapon named Brahmashira, worshipped by gods and Gandharvas.
Therefore, O descendant of Daśārha, just as you were toward my father, so now be toward me.
Having received that divine weapon from me, O best of the Yadus,
grant to me also your discus, the destroyer of enemies in battle.
O King, O bull of the Bharatas, as he stood with palms joined in reverence, begging me earnestly for a weapon from me, I too, being well-pleased, spoke to him:
"Gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, humans, birds, and serpents— "
Even if combined, they would not equal even a hundredth part of my prowess.
Here is this bow, this spear, this discus, and this mace;
whatever weapon you desire from me, that I shall give to you.
"Whatever you are able to lift up or even employ in battle—
take that, even without the weapon, which you desire to give to me.
He [then took] that iron wheel with a beautiful hub, a thousand spokes, and a vajra-like center.
"O mighty-armed one, he chose the discus, vying with me.
Immediately after I said, 'Take the discus,' he approached and suddenly seized the discus with his left hand."
But he was unable to move it from its place, O Acyuta;
then he proceeded to seize it with his right hand,
yet even with all his effort, he found it impossible to grasp.

Then, O Bhārata, having exerted the utmost effort and becoming utterly exhausted, the son of Droṇa— being deeply dejected— was unable to lift or even move that [stūpa], despite his entire army. He then desisted.
Then, having addressed the unconscious Aśvatthāman— who had desisted from that intention— I spoke to him very affectionately:
"He who has attained the status of the supreme authority among gods and men..."
The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, whose horses are white and whose banner bears the foremost of monkeys— he who,
desiring victory in single combat, gratified Śaṅkara, the blue-throated Lord of Umā, the manifest Lord of the gods.

"O Brahmin, since there is no other man on earth dearer to me than he, and since there is nothing— be it my wife or my sons— that I would not give to him, even by that Pārtha of unwearied deeds, my friend," so [he spoke].

"This speech which you address to me has never been spoken before. Having practiced a great and formidable vow of celibacy for twelve years, you— who were honored by me with ascetic penance— have come to the slopes of the Himalayas."
To Rukmiṇī, who observed the same vows as myself, was born my son named Pradyumna, a radiant being like Sanatkumāra. By him also was this great, divine, and peerless discus of mine [obtained].
"O fool, that which you have now requested was never before sought;
this which you have requested was never once uttered by the exceedingly powerful Rāma, nor by Gada, nor by Sāmba."
Neither by the inhabitants of Dvārakā nor by the other great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas has this ever been requested before, which you have now asked for; yet,
as the son of the preceptor of the Bhāratas, you are honored by all the Yādavas.
"You are not even capable of holding [this weapon], let alone hurling it in the great battle;
O best of chariot-warriors, my son, why indeed do you wish to fight with this discus?
Thus addressed by me, the son of Droṇa replied to me as follows.
"O Kṛṣṇa, having offered you worship, I shall fight with you. Then, O Lord, that discus worshipped by gods and dānavas was requested by you, saying, "May I be invincible"; I tell you this truly.
"O Keśava, O Govinda, having failed to obtain from you that desire which is so difficult to attain, I shall depart; bid me farewell with auspicious words.
This well-fashioned [discus] was borne by you, the bull among the Vṛṣṇis."
"No one else on earth can withstand my wheel, which has no rival wheel.
Having said this much, the son of Droṇa, like a child, took me, the chariot, the horses, the wealth,
and various jewels, and departed.
"He is impetuous, evil-minded, fickle, and indeed cruel; moreover, he knows the *Brahmaśiras* weapon. Therefore, Vṛkodara must be protected.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, that best of warriors, the delighter of all the Yādavas,
mounted his great chariot, which was equipped with the finest of all weapons and yoked to supreme Kāmboja horses adorned with golden garlands.
Sainya bore the right yoke-pole of that excellent chariot, which was the color of the rising sun; Sugrīva bore it on the left,
while Meghapuṣpa and Balāhaka were its two side-horses.
A divine banner-staff, fashioned by Viśvakarman and adorned with various jewels,
appeared as if it were rising high upon the chariot;
upon it stood Vainateya, radiant with a halo of rays.
The enemy of the serpents (Garuḍa) appeared as the banner of that Satyavat; following him ascended Hṛṣīkeśa, the banner of all archers,
along with Arjuna of true deeds and Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus.
Those two high-souled ones, standing on either side of the descendant of Daśārha,
graced him as he sat upon his chariot with the Śārṅga bow, like the two Aśvins beside Vāsava.
Having helped them both ascend that chariot honored by the world, the descendant of Daśārha [proceeded].
With a goad, he urged on the fleet-footed, supreme horses;
those steeds suddenly sprang forward,
carrying that excellent chariot occupied by the two sons of Pāṇḍu and the bull of the Yadus.
As those swift-moving horses bore the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
a great sound arose like that of birds swooping down.
O bull of the Bharatas, those tigers among men reached their destination in an instant.
Having swiftly pursued Bhīmasena, that great archer,
the sons of Kuntī who was blazing with wrath and prepared for the sake of his enemies,
those great car-warriors were unable to restrain him even though they had come together.
While those illustrious and firm-bowed warriors were looking on,
he proceeded toward the banks of the Bhagirathi with his exceedingly swift horses,
to where the son of Droṇa, the slayer of the high-souled princes, was said to be.
At the water's edge, he beheld the illustrious and high-souled Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa seated together with the ṛṣis;
and there was also that man of cruel deeds, anointed with ghee and clad in garments of kuśa grass.
He saw the son of Droṇa nearby, the ends of whose hair were covered with dust.
Grasping his bow and arrows, the mighty-armed Kaunteya Bhīmasena rushed toward him and cried out, "Stay! Stay!"
Seeing the one with the formidable bow grasping his bow,
and seeing his two brothers stationed behind him on Janārdana’s chariot,
the son of Droṇa became distressed in spirit and thought that his end had arrived.
Then that noble-souled son of Droṇa, filled with supreme rage and as if burning with anger, meditated upon that divine, supreme weapon;
and the son of Droṇa took up the reed-arrow with his left hand.
Having encountered that calamity, he invoked a divine weapon;
unable to endure those heroes standing there bearing celestial arms, he uttered these terrible words in rage: "May there be no Pāṇḍavas!"
Having spoken thus, O tiger among kings, the powerful son of Droṇa released that weapon for the purpose of deluding all the worlds. Thereupon,
fire was produced from within that blade of grass.
"Like Yama, the Ender of Time, at the end of an eon, he seemed as if he would consume the three worlds.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"By his very gesture, the descendant of Daśārha understood that intention from the very beginning."
Having learned of the son of Droṇa, the mighty-armed one addressed Arjuna:
"O Arjuna, O Arjuna, that divine weapon which resides in your heart,
taught by Droṇa— now, O Pāṇḍava, is the time for it."
"O Bhārata, for the sake of protecting your brothers and yourself,
you too must discharge this weapon that neutralizes other weapons in battle.
Thus addressed by Keśava, the Pāṇḍava, slayer of enemy heroes, [acted accordingly].

Taking up his bow along with arrows, the scorcher of foes quickly descended from the chariot; having first said "May it be well" to the preceptor’s son, then immediately to himself, and then to all his brothers.
Having paid homage to the deities and to his teachers in every way,
he released the Śiva weapon while meditating on it, saying, "Let this weapon be pacified by the [other] weapon.
Then that weapon was suddenly discharged by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
It blazed forth with great radiance, resembling the fire at the end of an eon;
likewise, that weapon of the fiercely energetic son of Droṇa blazed with mighty flames, enveloped in a circle of splendor.
There were many thunderclaps, and meteors fell by the thousands;
a great terror arose among all living beings. The sky became filled with sound and was intensely wreathed in garlands of flames.
The entire earth, together with its mountains, forests, and trees, trembled;
and as those two weapons remained there, scorching the worlds with their brilliance,
the two great seers appeared together at that place.
And that righteous-souled Nārada, the grandfather of the Bharatas—
both of them, those two sages who knew all dharma and desired the welfare of all beings, sought to pacify the two heroes, Bhāradvāja and Dhanañjaya.
Standing between those two blazing weapons,
the two illustrious and most radiant ones approached that interval; the two excellent sages remained there, like two flaming fires, invincible and full of splendor.
"Invincible by living beings and honored by gods and dānavas, [you two] have come to pacify the power of the weapons out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. Thus spoke the two sages.

"O great car-warrior, even those great car-warriors of the past who were experts in various weapons and have now passed away— though they acted with haste— they never, under any circumstances, discharged this divine arrow against human beings."
"What is this rash act that you two heroes have committed, which will bring such great calamity?
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Upon merely seeing those two, who were like fire in their splendor, the tiger among men..."
Reflecting that the time had come, the great car-warrior Dhanañjaya, wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, quickly withdrew that divine arrow. Then,
the best among speakers addressed those two sages with palms joined in reverence.
"I have indeed neutralized that discharged weapon with my own weapon, saying, 'Let it be pacified.
Now that this supreme weapon has been withdrawn, the evil-doing son of Droṇa will surely consume us all without exception by the fiery energy of his weapon."
"O you two who resemble gods, you ought to withdraw [this weapon] in such a way that what is beneficial for us and for all the worlds may prevail in every respect.
Having spoken thus, Dhanañjaya withdrew the weapon once again.

Indeed, even for the gods, it is difficult to withdraw that weapon once it has been released in battle; no one other than the Pāṇḍava— not even Indra himself— is capable of reclaiming that supreme weapon once it has been discharged in combat.

For that which is born of Brahmanic luster, once released by one of unrefined soul, cannot be turned back except through the vow of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). He who, having failed to observe the vow of celibacy, releases [the seed] and then seeks to withdraw it again—
That weapon severed the head of him along with his followers; yet Arjuna, though having obtained that weapon so difficult to acquire while observing the vow of celibacy,
did not release it even when afflicted by the greatest calamity.
The Pāṇḍava Arjuna, a hero who upholds the vow of truth, is a celibate student and one who serves his preceptor; therefore, he withdrew the weapon once again.
Then the son of Droṇa, beholding those two sages standing before him, [acted accordingly].
He was unable to withdraw that terrible weapon again in the battle;
being incapable of withdrawing that supreme weapon in the conflict,
O King, the son of Droṇa, with a dejected mind, addressed Dvaipāyana.
"O sage, afflicted by the most extreme calamity and desiring to save my life, I discharged this weapon out of fear of Bhīmasena. Furthermore,
unrighteousness was committed by me in my desire to slay the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
"O Blessed One, because Bhīmasena acted with deceitful conduct in battle, this weapon was released by me, O Brahmin, while my mind was not yet self-controlled. Therefore,
I do not venture here today to withdraw it once again."
"O sage, this divine and invincible weapon was indeed released by me after consecrating it with the fiery energy of Agni, saying, 'For the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas. Therefore,
it is now aimed at the end of the sons of Pāṇḍu."
"Today he will deprive all the sons of Pāṇḍu of their lives.
O Brahmin, this evil was committed by me with a mind possessed by rage,
as I released the weapon in battle, desiring the slaughter of the Pārthas."
Vyāsa said:
"O dear one, the wise Dhanañjaya Pārtha did not discharge the Brahmāśiras weapon out of anger, nor for the sake of slaying you in battle."
This weapon was discharged by Arjuna in battle while seeking to neutralize your weapon with his own, and it has now been withdrawn again;
for he obtained even this Brahmāstra through the instruction of your father.

The mighty-armed Dhanañjaya did not waver from the duties of a Kṣatriya. Why, then, do you desire the slaughter of this virtuous and steadfast man, who is skilled in all weapons and accompanied by his brothers and kinsmen?
When the Brahmashira weapon is countered by another supreme weapon,
the rain-god Parjanya does not pour rain upon that kingdom for twelve years.
For this reason, the mighty-armed Pandava, though he is powerful, [refrains from using it].

"O mighty-armed one, out of a desire to act for the welfare of all creatures, you must not discharge this weapon; the Pāṇḍavas, yourself, and the kingdom must always be protected by us. Therefore, withdraw this divine weapon."
"May you be free from anger, and may the sons of Pṛthā be free from affliction;
for the royal seer, the son of Pāṇḍu, does not wish to conquer through unrighteousness. Give back to them this jewel that rests upon your head."
"Taking this, the Pāṇḍavas will give back your life.
The son of Droṇa said:
"Whatever jewels belong to the Pāṇḍavas, and whatever other wealth belongs to the Kauravas—"
"Whatever has been obtained here by them, this jewel of mine excels them all;
for having fastened it on, there is no fear arising from weapons, disease, or hunger—
whether from gods, dānavas, or nāgas, in any way whatsoever."
There is no fear of hosts of rākṣasas, nor likewise any fear of thieves;
this jewel possesses such power that it must not be relinquished by me under any circumstances.
However, that which the Blessed One has told me must be performed by me immediately.
"This jewel and I, the reed, shall fall;
yet I am not able, O Blessed One, to withdraw it once it has been raised. Therefore, I discharge this weapon into the wombs."
"I shall not fail to carry out the word of the Blessed One, O Great Sage.
Then Vyāsa, deeply distressed in mind, spoke there to the son of Droṇa:
"This [weapon] that has been raised is infallible against the embryos of the Pāṇḍavas."
Vyāsa said:
"Do exactly this; you must never entertain any other thought. Having discharged this [semen] into the wombs of the Pāṇḍavas' wives, desist."
10,015.033 Vaiśampāyana said: Then Aśvatthāman, being greatly distressed upon hearing the words of Dvaipāyana, released that supreme weapon upon the embryos.
Hṛṣīkeśa, who is devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas, said to him:
"Setting aside only one future [offspring], let the weapon be discharged into the wombs;
I shall provide for these [others] one who will offer funeral cakes and increase their fame."

"Act thus toward the royal seer of meritorious deeds, who has performed many sacrifices; do not entertain any other thought whatsoever. By bringing about the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas from the very womb, you shall perish."
10,016.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having understood that [weapon] had been released by the evildoer, Hṛṣīkeśa,
rejoicing, then addressed these words to the son of Droṇa.
Formerly, seeing the daughter of Virāṭa— who was the daughter-in-law of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva— residing at Upaplavya, a Brahmin observing a vow said:
"When the Kurus have been utterly ruined, a son shall be born to you."
"This shall be his name, Parikṣit, while he is still in the womb;
the word of that virtuous man shall indeed come true,
for this son shall be their progenitor and restore the lineage."
To Govinda, the foremost of the Sātvatas, who was speaking thus at that time,
the son of Droṇa, highly incensed, replied with these words:
"It is not as you say, O Keśava, out of your partiality."
"O lotus-eyed one, my word shall not be otherwise. For this weapon, which was raised by me, will indeed fall upon the embryo of Virāṭa’s daughter,
O Kṛṣṇa, whom you wish to protect."
Vāsudeva said:
"The fall of that supreme weapon shall not be in vain;
let the child in the womb of Abhimanyu’s wife, Sṛñjayī, be saved."
"I shall restore this dead child to life;
though born dead, that embryo shall attain a long life.
Having been addressed thus, the son of Droṇa replied as if smiling:
"O Govinda, if you can revive one who has been burnt by a weapon, let it be so!
But all wise men know you to be a base and wicked man,
a perpetrator of evil deeds who repeatedly takes the lives of children."
"Therefore, you shall reap the fruit of this evil deed:
for three thousand years you shall wander this earth,
never obtaining any conversation whatsoever with anyone."

"Without a companion, you shall wander through desolate regions; for there can be no staying for you, O base one, in the midst of crowds of people. You shall be reeking with the stench of pus and blood, taking refuge in difficult wildernesses."
"O evil-souled one, you shall wander about afflicted by every disease.
But Parikṣit, having reached his youth and having obtained the Vedic vows,
that hero shall acquire all weapons through the grace of Śaradvat."
Having mastered the supreme weapons and remaining steadfast in the vows of the kṣatriya dharma,
that righteous-souled one shall protect the earth for sixty years. Beyond this time, the mighty-armed one shall become the king of the Kurus.

Having discharged his weapons, he departed from the banks of the Ganges toward the northern direction. O evil-minded one, while you were looking on, the king named Parikṣit was consumed by the fiery energy of my weapon; yet I shall restore him to life.
"O lowest of men, behold the power of my asceticism and of truth!
Vyāsa said:
"Since you have committed this cruel deed toward us, showing us no respect..."
Since you, though being a brahmin, have such conduct as this,
therefore that supreme word which the son of Devakī spoke will undoubtedly come to pass for you; go hence, O performer of base deeds!
Aśvatthāman said:
"O Brahmin, I shall remain among men together with you;
may this Blessed One, the Supreme Person, be true to his word."
10,016.019 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having then given the jewel to the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
the son of Droṇa departed for the forest with a heavy heart while they all looked on.
And the Pāṇḍavas, having slain their enemies, placed Govinda at their head,
as well as Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana and the great sage Nārada;
and with haste, they took the gem that had been born together with the son of Droṇa.
They rushed toward the high-minded Draupadī, who had resolved to fast unto death;
then those tigers among men, together with the descendant of Daśārha, returned once more to the camp on excellent horses that were like the wind.
Having swiftly descended from their chariots, those great car-warriors,
themselves even more afflicted than she, beheld the distressed Draupadī Kṛṣṇā.
Approaching her, who was joyless and overwhelmed by misery and grief, they stood there.
Surrounding him, the Pāṇḍavas together with Keśava stood there.
Then, permitted by the king, the mighty Bhīmasena gave him the divine jewel and spoke these words.

"O blessed lady, this jewel of yours has conquered the slayer of your son; he is defeated by you. Arise, cast off your grief, and remember the duty of a Kṣatriya, O dark-eyed one, at the departure of Vāsudeva for the sake of peace."
"O timid one, those words which you have spoken regarding the slayer of Madhu—
'I have no husbands, nor sons, nor brothers'—
you too, O Govinda, do not desire peace while the king [remains] here."

You have spoken wise words to the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) that are consistent with the duty of a Kṣatriya; you ought to remember them. The wicked Duryodhana, the obstacle to the kingdom, has been slain.

The blood of Duḥśāsana was drunk by me as he struggled; thus the debt of enmity has been discharged. Those who wish to speak should not be censured; having conquered him, the son of Droṇa was released out of respect for his status as a Brahmin.
"O Goddess, his fame has been cast down; only his body remains. He has been deprived of his jewel and laid low with his weapons upon the earth.
Draupadī said:
"I have attained complete freedom from my debt; the son of my preceptor is as my preceptor to me.
O Bhārata, let the king fasten this jewel upon his head.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, taking that [jewel], the king placed it upon his head at once,
even though it was the leavings of his preceptor, solely because of Draupadī’s words.
Thereafter, the lord bore that divine, excellent jewel upon his head.
That great king shone like a mountain with the moon;
then the high-minded Kṛṣṇā rose up, afflicted by grief for her sons,
and the King of Dharma questioned the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa.
10,017.001 Vaiśampāyana said: When all the troops had been slain during the night attack by those three chariot-warriors,
King Yudhiṣṭhira, grieving, spoke these words to the descendant of Daśārha.
"O Kṛṣṇa, how indeed were all my sons, those great car-warriors, slain by the wicked and base son of Droṇa, whose deeds are never weary?
For they were skilled in weapons, valiant, and capable of fighting hundreds and thousands."
And how could he [Kṛtavarman] slay Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
the best of chariot-warriors, whose very face the great archer Droṇa had never once turned toward in battle, and who was the son of Drupada himself, yet was struck down by the son of Droṇa?
"O bull among men, what deed must have been performed by that son of our preceptor, endowed with such power, that he alone has slain the entire camp? Vāsudeva said:
Surely that son of Droṇa sought refuge with the imperishable Lord of the lords of gods; for it was by him alone that he slew so many,
since when Mahādeva is pleased, he can even grant immortality.
And Giriśa would grant such vigor by which one might even strike down Indra.
For I know Mahādeva in truth, O bull of the Bharatas,
as well as his various ancient deeds.
O Bhārata, he is indeed the beginning, the middle, and the end of all beings;
this entire world moves by his very action. Thus desiring to create beings, the All-pervading Lord first beheld them.
The Grandfather said to him, "Create living beings without delay. Having replied,
"So be it," the golden-haired one, who perceived the defects of created beings,
performed austerities for a long time, submerged in the water, that great ascetic.
Then, after waiting for that very long time, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha),
the creator of all beings, produced another [being] from his mind.
Seeing Giriśa submerged in the water, he spoke to his father:
"If there is no other elder brother than I, then I shall create offspring. His father said to him, "There is no man other than you who is an elder brother;
this is Sthāṇu submerged in the water. Act with confidence and perform your task."
He created seven beings, the Prajāpatis beginning with Dakṣa,
by whom he differentiated this entire fourfold collection of living beings. As soon as they were created, all those creatures were hungry toward the Prajāpati.
O King, desiring to devour him, they then rushed forward with force.
Being devoured and seeking protection, he ran toward his grandfather, saying:
"May the Blessed One protect me from these; let a means of subsistence be ordained for them."

Then he gave them food, both stationary plants and moving beings, so that the weak might serve as food for the strong. Having been provided with this sustenance, those creatures departed satisfied to their respective homes.
Then, O King, they increased within their own wombs, full of joy.
When the multitude of beings had grown and the Teacher of the World was also gratified,
the eldest [son] rose from the water and beheld these creatures.
Seeing his offspring increasing in many forms through their own vital energy,
the Lord Rudra became enraged and pierced off his own *liṅga*.
When it was thus cast down upon the earth, it remained fixed there just as it was.
The imperishable Brahmā spoke to him, as if pacifying him with his words:
"O Śarva, what has been done by you who have remained in the water for so long?
And for what purpose was this linga uprooted and cast upon the ground?"
Then, filled with indignation, the Teacher of the World said to his Guru:
"These creatures have already been created by another; what indeed shall I do with them?
And this food, O Grandfather, was obtained by me through ascetic penance for the sake of my subjects."
"May the medicinal herbs perish just as living beings do.
Having spoken thus, the enraged Bhava, the great ascetic, departed with a troubled mind to the foot of Mount Muñjavat to perform austerities.
Vāsudeva said: Then,
when the age of the gods had passed, the gods indeed prepared a sacrifice according to the authority of the Vedas, desiring to perform it according to the prescribed rites.
Then, with undistracted minds, they prepared regions suitable for sacrifice,
as well as the deities entitled to portions and the sacrificial materials themselves. Indeed,
those deities did not know Rudra according to his true nature.

O lord of men, they did not allot a share for the god Sthāṇu. When no share was allotted to him in the sacrifice by the immortals, he, clad in animal skins and seeking his portion by force, first discharged his bow.
The sacrifice to the world, the sacrifice of ritual action, the eternal domestic sacrifice,
the sacrifice consisting of the five elements, and the fifth,
the sacrifice to men— seeking these sacrifices, Kapardin fashioned his bow.
O Bhārata, his bow was created with a length of five *kiṣkus*; the *vaṣaṭ* call became its string,
and the four limbs of the sacrifice formed its joints.
Then Mahādeva, filled with wrath, took up that bow and went to that very place where the gods were performing their sacrifice.
Seeing him, the eternal one, holding his bow and appearing as a celibate student (brahmacārin), they [were struck with wonder].
The goddess Earth trembled and the mountains shook;
the wind did not blow, and the fire, though fed with fuel, did not blaze. Furthermore, the circle of stars in the sky wandered about in agitation.
The sun did not shine, nor did the moon appear with its orb stripped of its splendor;
the entire sky became enveloped and overwhelmed by darkness.
Then the gods, being overcome, no longer perceived their respective domains.
The sacrifice did not manifest itself to them, and then the Vedas were lost.
Then he pierced the sacrifice in the heart with a fierce feathered arrow;
thereupon the sacrifice, having become a deer, fled away along with the sacrificial fire.
Having reached heaven in that very form, he shone brilliantly,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, as he was followed through the firmament by Rudra.
Once the sacrifice had departed from there, consciousness no longer manifested to the gods.
When the gods had lost consciousness, nothing at all could be discerned.
Enraged, Tryambaka shattered the arms of Savitṛ, the eyes of Bhaga, and the teeth of Pūṣan with the tip of his bow.
Then the gods and all the components of the sacrifice fled in every direction;
some there reeled about as if their lives had departed.
Having put them all to flight and having laughed aloud, the blue-throated one [Śiva]—
Then, seizing the tip of his bow, he obstructed the gods.
Thereupon, a voice uttered by the immortals severed the string of that bow.
Then, O King, that bow, its string suddenly cut, began to quiver.
Then the gods, together with the sacrifice, approached the god of gods who was now without his bow for refuge; and the Lord granted them grace.
Thereupon, being pleased, the Blessed One cast his wrath into a body of water.
O Lord, having become fire, he incessantly dries up the waters.
O Pāṇḍava, he restored the eyes of Bhaga, the two arms of Savitṛ, and the teeth of Pūṣan, and he restored the sacrifice as well.
Then all this world became healthy once again;
and the gods assigned all the sacrificial offerings to him as their share. O Lord, when he was angry, the entire world became unwell.
And when he was again composed and at ease, that powerful one became gracious toward him.
Then all those great car-warriors, your sons, were slain,
as well as many other heroes and the Pāñcālas along with their followers.
That should not be taken to heart, for it was not accomplished by the son of Droṇa; that was the grace of Mahādeva. Now perform what must be done next.
